counter_system.title: POS 1 — The Counter & the System
counter_system.desc: The foundation of the counter certification: the governed-centrally-trades-locally thesis, the four-piece anatomy and the local-copy design, the Point of Sale Profile previewed as the counter's constitution, the five roles with per-permission Power Approvers, the selling modes as separation-of-hands design, the laws inherited from seven tracks, and the trade's counter diseases — opening the Okelewo Stores case.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The eighth certification: the counter
lessons.html:
Seven tracks certified a firm's functions and the platform they stand on. This track certifies the place where all of it meets the PUBLIC: the counter — the till where the selling track's laws become keystrokes, the drawer where money custody is a physical fact, and the desk that is, in the trade's honest accounting, the firm's most attacked and least governed. The thesis that opens the eighth certification: the counter is governed centrally and trades locally — it runs on a profile, not on memory.

Why the counter needs its own certification. The argument, from both sides of the till: the counter is where the firm's money physically ARRIVES (every naira of retail revenue passes through a cashier's hands before it is anything else — the drawer is the firm's first custody point, and the money tracks' every discipline lands here in its rawest form), where the firm's REPUTATION is transacted (the receipt in the customer's hand, the return argued at the desk, the queue that moves or doesn't — the counter is the brand, hourly), and where the trade's FRAUD concentrates (the till is where sweethearting, void abuse, drawer skims, and discount collusion live — the whole catalogue this track's final module maps at full depth, because the counter's controls are only as real as the people certified to run and supervise them). And the counter has its own body of craft — the float discipline, the shift ritual, the override machinery, the offline judgment — that no other track teaches, because no other track sits at this desk.

The governing thesis. ZhiftPOS's design carries the academy's whole philosophy in one architectural sentence: everything a cashier is ALLOWED to do — whether they can discount, whether they can refund cash, whether a shift must open before selling, which payment methods appear — is decided CENTRALLY, on a record called the Point of Sale Profile, while the trading itself happens LOCALLY, on a terminal that keeps its own copy of the catalogue, prices and stock so that scanning stays instant and selling survives the line dropping entirely. Governed centrally: the policy is physics, set by named owners in the back office, not negotiated at the counter. Trades locally: the counter never stops for the network, because completed sales queue on the terminal and post when the link returns. The two halves of the sentence are the two halves of this track — the profile's constitution (module 2, the deep module) and the honest counter's daily proof (module 8, its equal).

The track's map. This module — the system's anatomy, roles, and selling modes. Module 2 — the Point of Sale Profile at ten-chapter depth: every tab, every access box, the Power Approvers. Module 3 — commissioning and the terminal estate. Module 4 — the shift and the sale: the counted float, the cart's craft, the close. Module 5 — concessions, returns and overrides: everything that takes money off or gives money back. Module 6 — the extended counters: Lay-By, Staff Purchase, Airtime, the Customer Desk. Module 7 — the voucher programme: stored value from mint to breakage. Module 8 — the honest counter: offline, the queue, reconciliation and supervision, at ten chapters. The laws will arc from the counter runs on a profile to the counter proves itself daily — and the case runs continuously through Okelewo Stores, a three-branch Abeokuta retailer whose counters this track takes from exercise books to a governed estate.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The four pieces: the system's anatomy
lessons.html:
Before any craft, the map: what the system actually IS — four pieces, each with a job, and a design decision underneath them that explains everything the counter does under pressure. The anatomy chapter.

The back office. The central web system — the home of items, prices, stock, customers, invoices and accounts: where administrators configure profiles, promotions, vouchers and staff access, and where finance sees the POSTED result of every sale. The back office is six earlier tracks' territory — the counter's relationship to it is the relationship this track governs: policy flows DOWN from it (the profile, the prices, the permissions), and money's evidence flows UP to it (the posted invoices, the shift closes, the reconciliations).

The till application. The installed desktop application the cashier actually uses — the Sales Console and every counter screen this track walks. Installed, not a browser tab: the distinction is load-bearing, because the installed application owns local state (below) in a way a web page cannot, and the counter's resilience is built on exactly that ownership.

The background sync service. The piece nobody sees and everybody depends on: a service that starts WITH THE TERMINAL and keeps running whether or not anyone is signed in — it owns the local copy of the catalogue, prices and stock, keeps them refreshed, and holds the queue of completed sales waiting to post. Because it is tied to the TERMINAL rather than to a cashier, signing out does not stop synchronisation — which yields the manual's own standing instruction, adopted here as doctrine: a terminal left on overnight still catches up on price changes and still posts queued sales, so never shut a terminal down purely to 'force a sync' — the restart superstition treats the system's most reliable piece as its least, and the certified professional retires it on day one.

The terminal management service. The optional fleet layer: head office seeing which tills are alive, pushing display settings, retiring a terminal that is lost or replaced — module 3's estate governance, given its machinery.

The local-copy design. The decision beneath the pieces, understood properly because half this track's judgments rest on it: the till is NOT a thin window onto the server — it keeps its own copy of the product catalogue, prices and stock on the terminal, so scanning and searching stay instant even on a slow line, and selling CONTINUES when the connection drops entirely, with completed sales queued locally and posted the moment the link returns. The design's two consequences, named now and governed later: the counter's SPEED and RESILIENCE are bought with local state (the cache that must be sized to the catalogue, the copies that can go stale — module 8's stock-stale and price-stale chips exist because copies age), and the counter's TRUTH is eventually consistent rather than instant (the queue means a completed sale and a posted sale are two moments — the gap this track teaches the counter to respect, never to fear: nothing in the queue is lost; the queue survives closing the application and restarting the terminal; and the discipline is simply that the gap is WATCHED and worked to zero, which is module 8's whole second half). The chapter's one-line summary for the site book: four pieces — the office that governs, the till that trades, the service that remembers, the fleet layer that watches — on a local-copy design that buys speed and resilience with discipline.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The profile: the counter's constitution, previewed
lessons.html:
The track's central record, met before its deep module so every chapter between can lean on it: the POINT OF SALE PROFILE — one record that governs one counter's entire behaviour. The preview chapter.

What the profile decides. The scope, stated to set the weight: whether a cashier can discount at all, and by which of three modes; whether cash can leave the drawer on a refund, or only store credit; whether a shift must be opened before a single item scans; which payment methods appear, and in what order; whether the counter sells vouchers, takes lay-bys, serves staff purchases, checks credit limits; who may approve what a cashier cannot do alone — every counter power on the list is a FIELD on the profile, which is the academy's oldest conviction arriving at its sharpest desk: the counter's policy is CONFIGURATION, decided by named owners in the back office, enforced by the machinery at 2 a.m. with nobody watching — the fence, not the memo, one more time, at the desk where the memo has historically governed everything.

Policy as physics, counter edition. The conviction's counter-specific force: at the trade's ungoverned tills, what a cashier may do is decided by folklore — the verbal rule about discounts, the supervisor's mood about returns, the shared understanding about the drawer — and folklore's enforcement is presence: the rules hold while someone senior is watching and dissolve when they are not. The profile replaces presence with physics: the discount control that is DISABLED is disabled for everyone including the persuasive; the return that requires an override requires it at closing time on a Saturday exactly as at noon on a Tuesday; and the hover-tooltip that explains WHY a control is disabled (the manual's own touch) turns every refusal into a policy citation instead of an argument. The consultant's implementation conversation writes itself from this paragraph: the owner who lists their counter rules aloud is reading out the profile's field list without knowing it — and the certified professional's job is the translation.

The first diagnostic. The profile preview closes with the track's most-used troubleshooting instinct, installed early because it answers half of all counter support questions: a menu item missing from the sidebar is a profile question, not a defect — the feature is off on the profile, or the cashier lacks the role or the access box on their row. The manual's own first-check discipline (check the profile tab that owns the feature, then the user's row) is this track's version of the Sysadmin track's permission-debugging method: systematic, two steps, and almost always right — the certified professional reaches for the profile before the restart, the reinstall, or the support ticket, because the profile is where the counter's behaviour LIVES, and module 2 is about to prove it field by field.

What the preview defers. The honest scoping line: this chapter establishes THAT the profile governs; module 2 — the track's first ten-chapter deep module — walks WHAT it governs, tab by tab: the setup defaults and cart rules, the three discount modes, payments and returns, the voucher tab's conservative machinery, the integrations, the per-user access boxes normalised by mode, and the Power Approver table that makes override a governed event. Between here and there, one instruction carries: every time a later chapter says 'where the profile permits', it is citing a field with an owner — and the certified reader should hear a decision, not a default.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The roles: who does what at the counter
lessons.html:
Five roles govern the counter's world — held on the user account in the back office, more than one per person where the firm is small. The roles chapter, joining the Sysadmin track's vocabulary at the counter's door.

The Point of Sale Administrator. The counter's configure authority: creates and maintains profiles, adds cashiers, sets discount policy, configures printers and hardware, commissions new terminals, installs updates — and reaches everything, including System Settings on the till itself. The role maps onto the Sysadmin track's custodian pattern deliberately: the POS Administrator is the platform track's admin wearing the counter's hat (at trade scale, often literally the same person), holding maximum capability under the same conduct standard — the configure pen used through the change disciplines, never for data acts, with the admin's own access on somebody else's review.

The Sales Manager. The trading day's supervisor: watches trading through the day, approves overrides, runs end-of-day reports, reconciles shifts — reaching the Command Center and Revenue Intelligence in addition to the selling screens. The role this track's final module certifies hardest, because supervision is where the counter's honesty is proven or lost: the manager who reads the variance report is a control; the manager who signs it unread is a signature.

The Cashier. The counter's working seat: opens a shift, sells, takes payment, handles returns if permitted, closes the shift — reaching the selling consoles their profile grants, plus Sales History, Customer Desk and Inventory Ops. The track's design honours the seat: module 4 is the cashier's own manual (the shift ritual, the cart's craft), written to certify the person, not merely describe the screens.

The Power Approver. The counter's override authority, and the track's most distinctive control: authorises the SPECIFIC sensitive actions assigned to them — discounts, returns, clearing a cart, changing a rate, overriding a credit limit — approving at the till by password, or by a one-time code sent to their email. The design's precision is the point: approver power is PER-PERMISSION (the person who can approve a return cannot thereby approve a rate change — five separate boxes, ticked deliberately), and the approval is an EVENT (who, what, when — the override trail that module 5 builds on and module 8's fraud map leans on). The role is the separation-of-hands law of six tracks, delivered at retail speed: the cashier proposes, the approver disposes, and the machinery remembers both.

The Voucher Manager. The stored-value programme's owner: creates voucher batches, sets voucher branding, monitors outstanding voucher liability — reaching the voucher records in the back office and the voucher console. Module 7's protagonist, previewed: the role exists because vouchers are MONEY (a liability from the moment one sells), and money's minting needs its own named custody.

The roles' governance. The chapter's closing disciplines, imported whole from the Sysadmin track and cited rather than re-argued: roles granted by events through the channel (the grant with an authoriser), reconciled at the walk (the access register's counter rows), and the first-check diagnostic repeated because it earns its repetition — the cashier missing a menu item is a role-or-access-box question before it is anything else. One counter-specific addition, stated now and enforced in module 4: one person, one account — the shared till login is the counter's original sin (every trail this track builds attributes acts to accounts, and the shared account makes the whole evidence layer read 'somebody'), and the certified counter retires it before the first shift opens.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The selling modes: how a sale flows
lessons.html:
Each profile is set to ONE selling mode, and the mode decides which consoles appear and how a sale flows from basket to payment. The modes chapter — where the counter's org design becomes configuration.

Standard. The usual shop counter: one person builds the basket and takes the money, on the Sales Console. The mode most of the trade runs, and the mode most of this track's chapters assume — one seat, whole sale, with the controls (overrides, approvers, the shift ritual) supplying the separation that the flow itself does not.

Pharmacy: the two-stage counter. The mode with a control inside it: one person assembles the order and hands it off (the Order Console); a SECOND person collects payment (the Checkout Console) — useful, as the manual says, where a dispenser and a cashier are different people, and read by this academy for what it structurally IS: the separation of hands, built into the sale's flow. The person who picks the goods does not touch the money; the person who touches the money did not pick the goods — the two-stage counter is the payroll track's preparer-approver law at retail speed, and the certified consultant recommends it not only where regulation expects it (the pharmacy trade's dispensing discipline) but wherever the goods-to-money handoff carries risk worth splitting: the checkout seat, notably, also carries Revenue Intelligence access — the money seat sees the money reports, by design.

Booking: reserve, then pay. The third flow: a sales representative reserves goods against a draft bill (the Booking Console); a cashier later collects payment and releases them (the Cashier Console). The showroom's mode — the negotiated sale, the customer who returns with the money — and structurally the same separation wearing sales clothes: the reserver and the collector are different seats, the draft and the payment different moments, and the flow gives the firm a governed answer to the trade's dangerous habit of 'keeping something aside' on memory.

Restaurant. Named for completeness and scoped honestly: table service with a kitchen display requires the separate restaurant edition — the retail edition this track covers does not include it, and the certified professional says so plainly rather than improvising a workaround.

The mode's governance. The disciplines that keep modes safe: the mode is settled FIRST when a profile is created (it controls which per-user access boxes are meaningful — the boxes are normalised against the mode on save, so a mode decided late scrambles access decided early), a LIVE profile's mode is changed only out of trading hours with every cashier row re-checked afterwards (the manual's own warning, adopted as ceremony: the mode switch resets the access boxes to match the new mode — a change that silently redraws who can do what, treated with module-5-of-Sysadmin weight), and the licence's precedence known (module 3 will detail it: the selling mode on the LICENCE takes precedence over the mode on the profile — a shop licensed for Standard presents the Standard console whatever the profile says, so the mode conversation includes the licence from the start). The chapter's closing frame: the mode is the counter's org chart expressed as a flow — one seat or two, sell-now or reserve-first — and choosing it is a design decision about separation and trust, made once, deliberately, before anything else on the profile.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The counter inherits the laws
lessons.html:
Seven tracks wrote laws; the counter is where most of them become physical. This chapter maps the inheritance — what the certified counter already owes the academy, before its own craft begins. The inheritance chapter.

Documents over memory, at retail speed. The academy's first conviction, at the desk that tests it hardest: every sale is a DOCUMENT from the moment it completes (the invoice with its reference, its lines, its payments — the counter's velocity changing nothing about the law), every return is a document against the original (module 5 will walk the find-invoice-first design: a return BEGINS by locating the sale it reverses, which is the document-against-document law built into the console's own three steps), and every override is an event with an author. The counter's folklore alternative — the exercise book, the verbal 'I'll sort it later', the return taken on a wave — is precisely what six tracks convicted, running at its highest transaction rate.

The registrar, at the receipt. The registrar's law lands on the counter twice: every sale carries its REFERENCE (the receipt's barcode and number — the retrievability that makes the return console's find-invoice step work, and makes 'the customer with a lost receipt' a Sales History search instead of a dispute), and the offline design honours it doubly (a sale completed offline prints with a LOCAL reference; once posted, the back-office reference takes over — both refer to the same sale, and a return can be found by either: two names, one identity, the registrar's discipline surviving the network).

Custody, at the drawer. The inventory track's custodian law, in cash: the drawer is the cashier's CUSTODY — taken over with a counted float (the opening count is the custody's signed receipt), held through the shift (the lock-the-till habit is the custodian stepping away from their store), and handed back with a counted close measured against expectation (the variance being the custody's reconciliation, green or red, explained in notes). Module 4 builds the ritual in full; this chapter names its ancestry: the cashier who counts before opening is the storekeeper signing the closing count before a transfer — the same law, in notes and coins.

Evidence, at the counter's pace. The evidence layer's counter form: the receipt as the customer-side evidence (printed, reprintable from Recent Receipts or Sales History — the reprint governed, because the receipt is a claim on the firm), the trails as the firm-side evidence (the override events, the shift closes, the markdown reasons — module 8's supervision reads them the way every track reads its registers), and the queue as evidence-in-transit (the completed-but-unposted sale being real money on its way to the ledger — held, watched, never lost, and worked to zero before handover: the manual's own conviction, 'conflicts and failed sales are real money that has not reached the ledger', arriving in this track as a load-bearing law).

The meshes ahead. The chapter closes with the track's deliberate joints, so the reader holds the map: Staff Purchase meshes the PAYROLL track (the purchase booked to the employee account and recovered through a salary component — module 6), End of Day Funds meshes ACCOUNTS (the counter's daily reconciliation feeding the bank reconciliation's expectations — module 8), the voucher programme meshes Accounts' liability discipline (module 7's whole spine), the terminal estate meshes SYSADMIN (module 3), and the counter's stock operations mesh INVENTORY (the material requests and transfers of module 6's Inventory Ops). The counter is not an eighth island — it is the place the archipelago touches the sea, and the certified professional works it holding all seven maps.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The trade's counter diseases
lessons.html:
What the certified counter replaces: the diseases every consultant meets at the trade's tills, catalogued before the cure so the cure's shape makes sense. The diseases chapter.

The exercise-book counter. The baseline disease: sales in a ruled notebook, prices from memory, the day's total whatever the book says it is — no line-level truth (which item, which price, which margin), no stock decrement (the warehouse and the counter drifting apart daily), and no dispute survivable (the customer's word against a pencil line). The book is not lazy — it is the pre-system optimum, and the consultant treats it with respect while replacing it completely: every later argument for the governed counter is an argument against a specific page of this book.

The shared login. The counter's original sin, named in Chapter 4 and convicted here: one account, four cashiers, every trail reading 'somebody' — the variance nobody owns, the override nobody made, the fraud map's every control dissolved at the root, because attribution is the precondition of every other discipline this track teaches. The cure is structural and cheap (one person, one account; the lock button between users on a shared terminal; the cached-cashier list making multi-user terminals workable offline), and it is ALWAYS the first fix, because nothing else holds without it.

The memory price and the mood discount. The pricing diseases as a pair: the price that lives in the seller's head (negotiated per customer, drifting per day — the selling track's price-list law violated at the till), and the discount granted by mood (unrecorded, unattributed, unbounded — the margin bleeding in amounts nobody can total because nothing was written). The governed counter's answer is module 5 entire: prices from the list, every concession carrying a reason and an authoriser, the markdown analytics telling the owner not just how much margin left, but WHY.

The unreconciled drawer. The custody disease: the float nobody counted, the close nobody measured, the drawer that is 'about right' — and the slow leak that thrives in 'about': the counter that never reconciles cannot distinguish error from theft, and so suffers both, unpriced. The cure is module 4's ritual (count open, count close, explain variance) plus module 8's supervision (the variance TREND read per cashier — the epistemics of every track, at the drawer).

The phantom return and the quiet void. The fraud pair, previewed for module 8's full map: the return processed with no customer present (money out of the drawer against goods that never came back), and the sale voided after the customer paid (the money pocketed, the record erased) — both thriving exactly where returns need no invoice, no reason, no approver, and no trail. The governed counter's answer is already visible in the product's design: the return that BEGINS at find-invoice, the reason list, the override requirement, the policy window — every step a wall this pair must now climb, and module 8 teaches the supervisor to watch the climbers.

The disconnected till. The last disease is the subtle one: the counter that has a system but is not OF the system — the standalone till whose sales are retyped into the books weekly, whose stock never decrements live, whose 'computerisation' is a printing upgrade. The manual's architecture is the cure by design (the till posting to the back office as sales complete, the office's policy flowing down as configuration) — and the consultant's diagnostic question is the chapter's closer: when a sale completes at your counter, what else happens, and when? The ungoverned answers — 'nothing', 'later', 'Blessing types them in' — are the engagement's opening findings, every time.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: Okelewo Stores takes the counter seriously
lessons.html:
The track's case firm, introduced — and its last ungoverned month, recorded honestly, because every module ahead repairs a line of it.

The firm. Okelewo Stores: a general retailer, three branches — the Okelewo Lalubu Road flagship in Abeokuta, a second Abeokuta shop, and a Lagos outlet — eleven counter staff across them, run for nine years on the founder's presence and the trade's standard instruments: exercise books at two branches, an aging standalone till at the flagship, prices in three heads, and a WhatsApp group standing in for every register this academy has ever named. The founder — the MD this case will follow — is a capable, suspicious, tired retailer who knows the counters leak and cannot say where: the profile of half the trade, and the reason this track exists.

The last ungoverned month. The findings walk, in the diseases' order: the EXERCISE BOOKS at the two smaller branches yield day totals that disagree with the cash by amounts nobody can decompose (the drawer 'about right' four days in five — the fifth day argued, never resolved); the flagship's standalone till runs ONE SHARED LOGIN for four cashiers (the variance report, where it exists, reads 'somebody' — a returns pattern the MD suspects and cannot attribute); prices at the Lagos shop drift from Abeokuta's by memory (the same item at three prices in one week — a customer with relatives in both cities makes it a reputation event); a RETURN is granted on a wave twice in the month (no invoice found, no reason recorded, cash out of the drawer — one certainly genuine, one the MD still wonders about); and the month's REAL margin is unknown at any level below 'the account balance moved'. The MD's note, opening the engagement and this case: I built three shops and I cannot tell you what any counter did on Tuesday. I am done managing by suspicion.

The decision and the cast. The engagement scopes exactly this track: ZhiftPOS across all three branches, on the governed pattern — and the roles are cast from the firm the academy's way: the operations lead (already the platform custodian in the firm's Sysadmin-track adoption) takes the POS Administrator hat (the counter's configure pen joining her existing conduct standard — two-account discipline and all); the flagship's senior supervisor becomes the Sales Manager whose certification module 8 will test hardest; four Power Approvers are named per-permission across the branches (the returns permission deliberately NOT given to everyone who holds the discount one — the per-box precision used as designed); the accountant takes the Voucher Manager role for the programme module 7 launches (stored value is money, and money's minting goes to the money seat); and every cashier gets their OWN account before anything else moves — the shared login retired as the engagement's act one, exactly as Chapter 7 demanded.

The map ahead. The deployment plan reads as the track's own table of contents, and closes the module: the profiles designed and built (module 2 — one per counter, the modes settled first: Standard everywhere, with the Lagos shop's pharmacy annex flagged for the two-stage mode's separation), the terminals commissioned and the estate registered (module 3 — the flagship's aging till replaced, branch locks set, the licence allowances mapped), the shift ritual installed with counted floats (module 4 — the MD buying the float boxes personally, which the consultant notes as the best possible sign), the concession machinery configured with markdown reasons and the approver table (module 5), the extended counters staged (module 6 — Lay-By first, by customer demand), the voucher programme launched for December (module 7 — the liability account opened before the first card is minted), and the supervision layer stood up last and forever (module 8 — the End of Day ritual, the fraud map briefed to the Sales Manager, the owner's page replacing suspicion with numbers). The MD's closing line for the module: so the counter gets a constitution, a ritual, and a daily proof. Nine years late. Begin.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the first law
lessons.html:
The orientation layer's scar tissue — the diseases of understanding that precede the diseases of practice. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — the thin-client assumption. Symptom: terminals restarted to 'force a sync'; panic when the line drops; the queue mistrusted and worked around. Disease: the local-copy design not understood (Ch. 2) — the till treated as a browser tab. Fix: the four-piece anatomy taught to every seat; the sync service's terminal-tied life known; the restart superstition retired on day one.

Pattern 2 — folklore governance. Symptom: counter rules that hold only under supervision; the discount policy as a verbal tradition; every refusal an argument. Disease: policy living in presence instead of the profile (Ch. 3). Fix: the profile as the counter's constitution — every rule a field with an owner, enforced by the machinery at 2 a.m., the disabled control's tooltip turning refusals into citations.

Pattern 3 — the shared login. Symptom: every trail reading 'somebody'; variances nobody owns; the fraud map's controls dissolved at the root. Disease: attribution never established (Ch. 4, 7) — the counter's original sin. Fix: one person, one account, before anything else moves; the lock button between users; the cached-cashier list making it workable.

Pattern 4 — the mode decided late. Symptom: access boxes scrambled after a mode switch; a two-stage counter run on a one-stage profile with 'trust' filling the gap; the licence's mode contradicting the profile's. Disease: the mode treated as cosmetic (Ch. 5). Fix: mode settled FIRST, changed only out of hours with every row re-checked, and the licence's precedence in the design conversation from the start.

Pattern 5 — the counter as an island. Symptom: sales retyped into the books; stock decremented weekly by guess; the till 'computerised' but disconnected; seven tracks' laws stopping at the shop door. Disease: the inheritance refused (Ch. 6, 7). Fix: the counter run as the place the firm's laws become physical — documents at retail speed, custody at the drawer, evidence at the receipt, and the meshes to Payroll, Accounts, Inventory and Sysadmin wired deliberately.

Pattern 6 — managing by suspicion. Symptom: the owner who knows the counters leak and cannot say where; accusations without attribution; good staff resented and bad staff undetected, at once. Disease: no instrument between trust and doubt (Ch. 7, 8). Fix: this track entire — the constitution, the ritual, the daily proof — because the governed counter's deepest gift is not catching the guilty but CLEARING the honest, hourly, by record.

The first law. The eighth track opens where its product's architecture points: the counter is governed centrally and trades locally — every counter power a profile field with a named owner, every seat an attributed account, the mode a design decision made first, the local copy trusted and watched, and the queue respected as money in transit. Module 2 now opens the constitution itself: the Point of Sale Profile, at ten-chapter depth — every tab, every box, every approver.

pos_profile.title: POS 2 — The Point of Sale Profile
pos_profile.desc: The track's first deep module: the counter's constitution at field depth — the ten-record groundwork with the sanity-check sale, items/prices/tax with the one-template-one-behaviour law, tab one's operating posture, the discount constitution and override economics, payments/returns/lay-by/staff purchase, the voucher tab's deliberate conservatism with Guarded Offline as a risk budget, integrations, the access rows normalised by mode, and the Power Approver table staffed and rehearsed.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — One record, one counter: the constitution
lessons.html:
The deep module opens on the record everything else in this track obeys: the POINT OF SALE PROFILE — one record governing one counter's entire behaviour, its settings grouped into five tabs, every field a policy with an owner. The constitution chapter.

The constitutional frame. The academy's settings-walk discipline, arriving at its richest single record: the profile is walked field by field at implementation (every consequential default converted from an accident into a decision — the defaults-are-decisions law of the Sysadmin track, at the counter), its answers recorded with their reasons and deciders (the configuration record's counter page), changes travel the change ceremony (the profile edit is a policy edit — the discount mode switched casually is a constitutional amendment made in a corridor), and the corridor toggle stands convicted in advance in its counter clothes: the return window 'extended for one customer', the override requirement 'lifted for the busy season', the negative-stock permission 'enabled temporarily' — each an amendment that computes for every sale thereafter, remembered by no one, found by the walk or by the loss.

Profile per counter, or per shop? The module's first design decision, taken from the manual's own guidance and given the academy's reasoning: ONE PROFILE PER COUNTER where tills need different hardware behaviour, different opening floats or different permissions; ONE SHARED PROFILE where every till in a shop should behave identically — far less to maintain, with terminals still distinguished individually for reporting. The decision test, stated for the consultant: the profile count follows the POLICY count, not the terminal count (three identical tills under one policy is one profile; the till by the door that also handles returns is a second policy and earns its own record) — the role-catalogue logic of the Sysadmin track, at the counter: few records, purpose-clear, each one a policy-shape that exists because a policy-shape exists.

The module's map. Ten chapters, the track's first deep module: the groundwork the profile points at (2), the items, prices and tax beneath it (3), Tab one's setup fields (4), Tab two — the discount constitution, the profile's most consequential ground (5), Tab three — payments, returns, lay-by and staff purchase (6), Tab four — the voucher tab's deliberate conservatism (7), Tab five plus the users table and the Power Approvers (8), Okelewo's profiles built (9), and the patterns and the law (10). One voice discipline governs throughout, inherited and enforced: the profile's fields are decided by their OWNING functions (the discount mode is a margin policy — selling's owner decides; the cash-refund switch is a treasury policy; the voucher caps are the money seat's) with the administrator holding the pen — the configure authority executing decisions, never making them, which is the authority map of two tracks, at the record where its breach is most tempting because the pen sits so close to the counter's daily noise.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The groundwork: ten records before one profile
lessons.html:
The profile points at records that must already exist — and the manual's warning is this chapter's thesis: get these right first and the profile takes ten minutes; get them wrong and you will be unpicking postings for a week. The groundwork chapter.

The checklist, in order. The ten records, walked with their reasons: the COMPANY (the legal entity that will own the sales — its default currency and chart confirmed: the counter posts into the Accounts track's world, and posts into the WRONG company are the week of unpicking incarnate), the COST CENTRE (where the shop's trading lands — one per branch as the chains' standard: the dimension the Accounts track's branch views harvest), the WAREHOUSE (the stock location the till sells from — a LEAF warehouse, never a group: the till can only sell what this warehouse holds, and the leaf-not-group rule is the Inventory track's custody law expressed as a validation), the BRANCH (the shop itself — the record a terminal gets LOCKED to, its three fields tying company, warehouse and cost centre into one anchor: named clearly enough that nobody commissioning a terminal picks the wrong one, because the wrong pick is an administrator-verified unlock away from correction), the PRICE LIST (selling, in the company currency, with rates loaded — Chapter 3's validity discipline), the TAX TEMPLATE (the profile will not save without one — the statutory carrier, per Chapter 3), the PAYMENT METHODS (one record per way money arrives — Chapter 3's special three), the CUSTOMER GROUP and TERRITORY defaults (where walk-ins are filed — the master hygiene of the data tracks, pre-decided), the WALK-IN CUSTOMER (the record unnamed sales book to — one, deliberate, not a per-cashier improvisation), and the USER ACCOUNTS (one per cashier, each with a working email and a password they know — module 1's one-person-one-account law as a checklist line, with the email load-bearing because the one-time-code machinery of Chapter 8 delivers to it).

The sanity check. The manual's own pre-commissioning discipline, adopted as the academy's rehearsal instinct: before commissioning a terminal, sell ONE item end to end from the back office against the same warehouse and tax template — if that posts cleanly, the till will too. The check's logic taught, not just its steps: the till is a fast front end onto the same posting machinery, so the back-office sale exercises the whole chain (the item, the price, the tax, the warehouse, the accounts) with none of the till's variables — the failure isolated to the groundwork BEFORE the terminal adds its own layer, which is the nothing-first-in-production law wearing retail clothes.

The groundwork's custody. The chapter's closing split, per the standing map: every checklist record has its OWNING track and pen (the company and chart are the accountant's, the warehouse and branch inventory's, the price list selling's, the accounts wiring finance's) — the POS implementation does not CREATE this world; it points a counter at a world seven tracks already govern, and the consultant who finds the groundwork absent has found the engagement's real scope: the counter that seems to need a till often needs a chart, a warehouse discipline, and a price list first, and the certified professional prices the foundation before the furniture.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Items, prices, tax & tender: the counter's raw materials
lessons.html:
Beneath the profile, the records every scan touches: the items with their flags, the prices with their windows, the tax template the bill is computed by, and the payment methods money arrives through. The raw-materials chapter.

Items: the flags that matter at the till. The item record's counter-consequential fields: the BARCODE (if the shop scans) and a sensible SHORT NAME (long names truncate in the cart — legibility as configuration), the TAXABLE flag (on for standard-rated goods, off for exempt lines — honoured PER LINE by the till: the mixed basket taxed correctly because each line carries its own answer), the BATCH/SERIAL setup (an item tracked by batch or serial must be BORN that way in the item record, or the till cannot ask the cashier which batch or serial is being sold — the tracking decision is a birth decision, per the master tracks' law), NON-STOCK items supported (services and fees, unheld by stock checks), and KIOSK flags (the items shown when a terminal switches to kiosk mode).

Prices: the validity-window discipline. The pricing rules with the disease they prevent: rates loaded against the profile's selling price list (an item with NO rate scans at ZERO — flagged by the till but not blocked: the zero-rated scan being the counter's classic silent leak, sold at nil while everyone assumes a price), the validity window read properly (a rate whose start date has not begun, or whose end date has passed, is treated as NO RATE AT ALL — the manual's own diagnosis for 'items ringing up at nil', and this track's standing first-check for pricing complaints), BATCH prices preferred over the list rate where a batch carries its own, and the refresh discipline known (price changes reach terminals on the next price refresh — no restarts, per module 1's retired superstition).

Tax: one template, one behaviour. The template law, taught with its trap: the profile names a sales tax template, and tax is calculated BY THE TEMPLATE at the moment the bill is created — with two interacting settings: Is Tax Inclusive on the profile (shelf prices already contain tax) and the per-item Taxable flag. The trap is structural and the manual names it plainly: switching the inclusive setting REWRITES THE SHARED TEMPLATE (its lines marked as included in the printed rate, or reversed) — so two profiles with OPPOSITE tax treatments pointed at the SAME template will fight over it, each save rewriting the other's behaviour: give each treatment its own template — the one-template-one-behaviour law, and a first-class example of this academy's blast-radius instinct: the setting that silently edits a shared record is a setting whose radius must be known before it is touched.

Payment methods: the special three. Every tender is a payment method record added to the profile's payments table — the TABLE ORDER being the DISPLAY ORDER cashiers see (a policy, not an accident: cash first because cash is fastest is a decision someone makes) — and three names carry special behaviour: Cash (prompts for the amount tendered, calculates change, opens the drawer, works OFFLINE), Store Credit (draws down the customer's balance — requires the server to confirm it, so UNAVAILABLE offline: the balance that cannot be verified from a local copy, the design honesty module 8 builds on), and Gift Voucher (appears automatically when vouchers are enabled, positioned after cash and card — module 7's tender). Card, transfer and their kin simply RECORD the amount — no live call, so they work offline — with the integrated card terminal being the exception Chapter 8's integrations tab governs. The chapter's closing line: the raw materials are seven tracks' masters meeting one screen — and every counter complaint that begins 'the till is wrong' ends, four times in five, at a flag, a window, a template, or a table order that was never decided.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Tab one: setup — the counter's operating posture
lessons.html:
The first tab: the defaults, the cart's rules, the stock posture, the shift machinery, and the terminal switches — the counter's operating posture, field by field. The setup chapter.

Defaults. The walk-in machinery's settings: the DEFAULT customer group and territory (where counter-created customers are filed — the master hygiene pre-decided so eleven cashiers file identically), Allow Duplicate Customer Names (OFF refuses a second customer with an existing name — the dedup-at-birth guard of the master tracks as a checkbox: turned on only where genuinely common names cause repeated blocks, and turned on as a DECISION with the merge tool's monthly scan as its compensating control), and Max Items in Search Results (the grid kept snappy on modest hardware — performance as configuration).

The cart's rules. The basket's governance: Allow Clear Cart with its approver interplay read precisely (when OFF, the Clear button still appears IF a Power Approver holds the clear-cart permission — but requires approval: the design that makes 'discard this basket' an authorised event rather than an impossible one, because the clear-cart power matters to module 8's fraud map — the basket built, paid in cash, and cleared instead of completed is the quiet void's mechanism, and the approval requirement is its wall), Clear Cart On Logout (off where shifts hand over mid-basket; on where an abandoned basket must never carry to the next person — a custody decision), Allow Checkout Item Update (quantities changeable on the payment screen — convenience weighed against the review discipline of building the cart right), the queue/stack toggle (Enable Item Queue Options — stack merges a re-scan into the existing line; queue makes each scan its own line, suiting counters where each unit needs its own serial or batch), and the held-basket HOUSEKEEPING pair (Delete Cart Queue + Delete After days — the parked baskets aged out automatically: the museum discipline, at the hold shelf).

Inventory and stock. The stock posture's three: Allow Viewing Other Warehouses (the 'do you have it at the other shop?' answered from Inventory Ops without a phone call — need-to-know widened deliberately, per branch design), Allow Negative Stock (selling what the system believes is absent — MIRRORING a company-wide stock setting and refusing to save unless that setting also permits it: the two-lock design read correctly — the profile cannot quietly grant what the Inventory track's constitution forbids, and the certified consultant treats the request to enable it as the Inventory-track conversation it actually is), and Enable Auto Allocate Batch (batches picked automatically, OLDEST FIRST, asking only when the quantity cannot be covered — FEFO as a speed setting: the busy counter's throughput bought at the cost of manual control, decided by the goods' nature — the pharmacy's expiry discipline wants it on; the counter selling mixed provenance may want the ask).

Shift, terminal and access. The remaining posture: Enable Shift Management (a shift must open before selling and close with a counted drawer — module 4's whole ritual, switched here: the counter that handles cash turns it ON, and the consultant treats OFF as an exception needing a reason), Enable Offline Login (sign-in against the terminal's local record when the server is unreachable — prior successful online sign-in on THAT terminal required, expiring seven days after the last one: recommended ON for any shop with unreliable power or connectivity, because the cashier signed out when the line drops otherwise cannot sell at all), Enable Kiosk Mode, Enable Messages (the Message Hub — off at counters that should not handle transfer requests: the channel scoped per seat), Allow Transaction Date Edit (back-dating a sale, future dates never — granted SPARINGLY because it moves revenue between reporting days: the period-integrity law of the Accounts track guarding a checkbox), and Enable Airtime Sales (module 6's console, switched per counter). The chapter's cadence line: tab one is where the counter's daily FEEL is decided — and every field just walked is a feel someone will live with hourly, which is exactly why each one gets an owner and a reason before it gets a tick.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Tab two: the discount constitution
lessons.html:
The manual's own words set this chapter's weight: Discount Mode is the single most consequential setting on the profile — it decides how a cashier is allowed to take money off a line, which is to say it decides how the firm's margin is governed at the moment of pressure. The discount chapter.

The three modes. Walked as the margin-governance designs they are: STANDARD — the cashier types a discount directly on the line, clearing it with an approver at the moment of discounting where an override is required (suits the small shop with the supervisor on the floor — governance by proximity, honest about its dependency: the mode works exactly as well as the approver's presence), APPROVAL-BASED — every discount must carry a REASON chosen from the markdown list plus a typed explanation, so nothing is discounted without a stated cause and the margin report tells you WHY (suits chains that need every markdown attributed — the mode this academy recommends as the trade default, because it converts the margin's leak from a number into a diagnosis: module 5 of this track builds the markdown-reason craft on it), and CODE-BASED — the cashier cannot type a discount at all; they raise a request from the cart, a category lead approves it centrally (optionally changing the amount), and the cashier applies the returned code, with every stage timestamped and the code reserved against that cashier so two tills cannot consume one approval (suits high-value goods where every concession is negotiated — the strongest separation, at the cost of round-trip latency, and the full cycle is module 5's terrain). The selection judgment stated: the mode follows the GOODS and the FLOOR (the supermarket's velocity, the boutique's negotiation, the electronics counter's ticket sizes), it is chosen by the margin's owner, and it is the profile's one field the consultant never lets default.

The override economics. The authorisation channel's honest trade, from the manual's own comparison: Password approval is faster and works OFFLINE, but requires the approver physically present; One-Time Code lets a manager approve from anywhere by reading six digits down the phone — but the terminal must be ONLINE to request one, every approver holding the permission receives the email, and codes expire after an hour. The design consequences drawn: the branch with a resident supervisor runs password; the branch whose approvers travel runs codes and accepts the online dependency; and the all-approvers-emailed behaviour is read as the audit feature it is — every code request is announced to every holder, so the quiet code extracted from one friendly approver does not exist as a category.

The remaining pricing fields. The tab's other switches, each with its weight: Allow Discount Edit (the MASTER switch — off disables the discount control on every line regardless of mode: the counter that simply does not discount, expressed as one field), Allow Rate Edit and Require Override for Rate Edit (overwriting the unit price outright — the stronger power than discounting, marked on the line as Rate override for review, and the require-override companion treated as near-mandatory wherever rate editing is allowed at all: the unmarked rate change is the memory-price disease of module 1 readmitted through a checkbox), Enable Promotions and Enable Promotion Code (the automatic campaign machinery and its manual-code companion — module 5's promotions, switched here, with the lock-the-line behaviour previewed: a promotional discount on a line closes that line to further manual concession), Is Tax Inclusive (Chapter 3's shared-template law, cited not repeated), and Allow Shipping Cost (the editable delivery fee line — a priced service, not a discount vector, and watched as such). The chapter's closing conviction: the discount tab is where the margin's constitution lives — and the firm that cannot say which mode it runs, who approves, and by which channel has not chosen a discount policy; it has inherited one, and the inheritance is always the most permissive accident available.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Tab three: payments, returns, lay-by & staff purchase
lessons.html:
The third tab governs money's edge cases: the partial payment, the credit limit, the loyalty switch — and then the tab's heavy machinery: returns, lay-by and staff purchase, each a module of this track configured here. The money-edges chapter.

Customer and payment. The four switches: Allow Partial Payment (a sale completing with less than full tender, the balance owing on the customer's account — the counter issuing CREDIT, which is the Selling track's credit discipline arriving at a checkbox: switched on only where the credit machinery behind it is real), Enable Credit Limit Check (the customer's balance and limit on the cart header, selling SUSPENDED when the limit is breached — 'Sales suspended due to customer outstanding' — releasable only by a Power Approver holding the credit-limit permission: the credit fence as physics, with the release as an authorised event), Allow Customer Credit Against Invoice (the unpaid balance carried on the invoice itself), and Allow Loyalty Points (earn and redeem at this counter — redemption calculated on the SERVER, so unavailable offline: the balance-verification honesty, again).

The returns block. Money's reverse gear, configured conservatively: Allow Cash Refund (money back OUT of the drawer — when OFF, the only refund route is STORE CREDIT: the default posture this academy endorses for new deployments, because store credit keeps the refund inside the firm's ledger while cash refund opens the drawer to module 8's phantom-return mechanism; cash refund is enabled as a deliberate step with its override companion), Allow Return Exchange (goods swapped for goods, the difference settled either way), Require Override for Returns with its Return Override Mode (every return an authorised event — password or code, per Chapter 5's economics), and the Global Return Policy pair (the time limit enforced — Return Policy In Days, default thirty, with returns BEYOND the window still possible but requiring an override: the policy window as a soft fence with a governed gate, not a wall). The console-visibility rule read precisely, because it answers a standing support question: the Return & Exchange console appears when ANY of cash refund, exchange or the global policy is enabled — none enabled, no console at all: the sidebar as the profile's mirror, one more time.

Lay-by. The reservation machinery's three numbers: Lay-By Deposit % (the minimum taken at creation — default ten), Lay-By Installments (how many the balance splits into — default three), and Lay-By Day Spacing (comma-separated days from booking on which instalments fall due — the supplied 0, 30, 90 meaning now, a month, three months), with the reconciliation rule known: where spacing values and instalment count disagree, the COUNT wins and the schedule fills from the values available — provide as many spacings as instalments, and treat the mismatch as a configuration error to fix, not a behaviour to rely on. Module 6 runs the console; this tab decides its arithmetic — and the arithmetic is a CREDIT policy (the deposit is the firm's protection against the reserved-then-abandoned basket) decided by the margin's owner, not defaulted.

Staff purchase. The two profile fields with their company-wide companions: Enable Staff Purchase (the console switched per counter) and Staff Purchase Discount % (applied automatically to every line — with the PRECEDENCE rule known: the per-profile percentage takes precedence over the company-wide staff discount at this counter), and the dependency map completed from the manual: employees need a PURCHASE LIMIT on their employee record, and the company-wide settings must name the employee purchase ACCOUNT and the payroll SALARY COMPONENT used for recovery — the Payroll track's variable-pay law wired into the counter's configuration, with module 6 running the flow. The chapter's closing frame: tab three is the counter's credit desk — every switch on it either lets money leave later, leave backwards, or leave discounted — and each one is therefore a treasury decision wearing a checkbox, owned accordingly.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Tab four: the voucher tab — deliberate conservatism
lessons.html:
The manual sets this tab's tone in one sentence, and the academy adopts it whole: gift vouchers are BEARER INSTRUMENTS — a customer buys one and anyone holding the code can spend it — so because they are money, everything here is deliberately conservative and OFF until you turn it on. The voucher-configuration chapter (the programme itself is module 7; this chapter is its constitution).

The core switches. The tab's foundation: Enable Gift Voucher (the master switch — the voucher tile on the Sales Console and Gift Voucher as a payment method, positioned after cash and card), Voucher Denominations (the face values offered as quick buttons — comma-separated, with cashiers still able to type another amount: the presets as friction-reduction, not limits), Enable Voucher Partial Redemption (a voucher worth more than the bill leaving a BALANCE instead of being consumed whole), and the Voucher Change Policy (the surplus's fate when a voucher exceeds the bill: Remainder as Balance keeps it on the voucher; No Change forfeits it — a customer-fairness policy with a breakage consequence, decided by the programme's owner and printed into the customer's expectations).

The offline policy: the tab's hardest thinking. The design taught as the exemplar it is: a voucher balance CANNOT be verified from a local copy — so Voucher Offline Policy defaults to Online Only (voucher activity refused while the terminal cannot reach the server, the cashier told plainly — the safe choice, and the refusal is intentional, not a defect), with Guarded Offline as the deliberate alternative: voucher activity permitted within TWO CAPS — the Offline Max Value (the largest single voucher redeemable offline) and the Offline Daily Cap (the total voucher value one terminal may redeem offline in a day). The design read in the academy's language: Guarded Offline is a RISK BUDGET — the firm pricing its maximum exposure to the double-spend window and buying continuity with it — and the certified consultant sets the caps in that conversation (what is the worst day worth?), never as round numbers, and revisits them as the programme's volumes grow.

The extended switches. The remaining machinery, each off-by-default and each a policy: Enable Voucher Top-up (adding value to an existing voucher — the stored-value account deepened), Enable Voucher Expiry (vouchers carrying an expiry date and stopping after it — the breakage clock of module 7's accounting, switched here), Enable Corporate Vouchers (bulk issues to a named corporate customer — module 7's batch machinery serving them), Enable Refund to Voucher (a gift voucher as a refund destination on returns — the store-credit posture's sibling, keeping the refund as stored value), Allow Voucher Buy-back (the shop redeeming an unspent voucher for CASH — the tab's most dangerous switch, because it converts a bearer instrument directly into drawer cash: enabled only with the override and supervision machinery around it, and module 7's fraud map treats it as a named surface), and Enforce Voucher Booking (a voucher reserved centrally before issue at the counter — closing the window in which two tills could issue the SAME code: the double-issue race, closed by design, and the switch the multi-till shop turns on as a matter of course).

The tab's law. The closing frame, joining Chapter 3's tender rules: unless Guarded Offline was deliberately chosen, any sale that either SELLS or REDEEMS a voucher is refused offline — and the cashier is told so plainly, which is the design's honesty doing the training. The voucher tab is the academy's conservatism made visible: every default protects the money, every enablement is a decision with an owner, and the consultant who finds this tab configured by enthusiasm — everything on, caps blank, buy-back live — has found module 7's first remediation item before the programme has sold a card.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Tab five, the users table & the Power Approvers
lessons.html:
The constitution's final ground: the integrations tab, the cashiers' access rows, and the approver table that makes override a governed event. The access chapter.

Tab five: integrations. The card terminal's wiring, with its commissioning discipline: Enable Payment Gateway (the integrated terminal — a card payment PUSHED to the device, the till waiting for the result rather than the cashier keying it), the Live Environment switch with the manual's own ceremony adopted verbatim: commission with it OFF (pointing at the test environment), PROVE a test transaction, THEN switch — the nothing-first-in-production law at the payment rail, and the switch's state recorded in the change log both times; the credentials (merchant identifier, public key, private key — the private key stored MASKED, and all three under the Sysadmin track's credential custody: governed storage, rotation by events, never ambient), and the Terminals table (one row per physical card terminal, so the till knows which device receives a payment — the estate's map, per counter). The offline honesty repeated where it bites: an integrated card payment needs a live call — offline, the cashier is told to use cash, a manually keyed card entry, or transfer.

The users table. One row per person who signs in at this counter, each carrying the account and its ACCESS BOXES: Standard (the Sales Console — ordinary selling), Order and Checkout (Pharmacy mode's two stages — with Checkout also granting Revenue Intelligence: the money seat sees the money reports, by design), Booking and Cashier (Booking mode's pair), and Inventory Ops (stock enquiry, material requests and transfers — on by default). The table's mechanics known precisely: the boxes are NORMALISED against the profile's mode on save (Standard mode grants everyone Standard and clears the two-stage boxes; Pharmacy clears the booking boxes — which is WHY module 1 said mode is settled first), one row per profile is marked as the user's DEFAULT (the profile they sign into automatically), and the LANDING rule known for support: the till opens on the first console the person is entitled to — Sales in Standard, Checkout-or-Order in Pharmacy, Cashier-or-Booking in Booking, and someone with only Inventory Ops lands there. The row is the counter's access register entry — granted by events, reconciled at the walk, per two tracks' standing law.

The Power Approvers. The override machinery, complete: one row per approver, ticking ONLY the permissions they should hold — Discount, Returns (including returns outside the policy window), Clear Cart, Rate, and Credit Limit Override — five separate boxes, per module 1's per-permission precision. The prompt's mechanics: the approver's EMAIL and PASSWORD at the till, or the ONE-TIME CODE per the action's override mode — six digits, emailed to EVERY approver holding the relevant permission, expiring after an hour. And the failure mode the manual names, adopted as a commissioning check: no approvers, no override — if a profile requires an override for an action but no approver holds that permission, the control is DISABLED and the cashier is told there are no approvers configured: always add at least one, and the certified consultant's go-live checklist tests every override path with a real approval before the first customer, because the discount that cannot be approved at 6 p.m. on launch day is a queue, a scene, and a corridor toggle waiting to be offered.

The constitution, closed. The chapter ends the walk with the module's discipline restated once: five tabs, one users table, one approver table — every field now walked has an owner, a reason, and a recorded answer, and the profile that emerges is not a configuration but a CONSTITUTION: the counter's policy, written where the machinery enforces it. Chapter 9 watches Okelewo write theirs.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Case study: Okelewo writes its constitution
lessons.html:
Three counters, three profiles, one afternoon of decisions that will govern years. Every chapter clocks in.

The groundwork walked (Ch. 2-3). The ten-record checklist runs first and finds the expected gaps: the Lagos shop has no leaf warehouse (a group warehouse stood in — corrected through Inventory's owner), the price list carries forty items with EXPIRED validity windows (the zero-rated-scan disease, latent — the windows fixed and the quarterly price-list review added to selling's calendar), and the tax check catches the module's signature trap in the wild: the draft plan pointed BOTH the tax-inclusive flagship AND the tax-exclusive Lagos counter at ONE template — split into two before the first save, the one-template-one-behaviour law applied on paper instead of discovered in production. The sanity-check sale posts cleanly from the back office at each branch; the payments table is ordered deliberately (cash, transfer, card — the floor's actual frequency); and eleven user accounts exist with working emails before any profile names them.

The profiles decided (Ch. 1, 4-6). The profile count follows the policy count: THREE profiles — one per shop, shared across each shop's tills (identical policy within a branch; the flagship's returns-handling till deferred as a possible fourth when module 5's volumes justify it). Tab one's posture: shift management ON everywhere (the counted drawer is the engagement's spine), offline login ON (Abeokuta's power reality), auto-allocate batch ON at the flagship's provisions counter (FEFO for the expiring goods) and OFF at the Lagos electronics wall (serials want the ask), transaction-date edit OFF for everyone (the period-integrity default, with the MD's one 'but sometimes—' answered by the reporting-days argument and withdrawn), duplicate-name refusal ON with the monthly merge scan as its companion. Tab two: Approval-based discount mode at all three (the margin diagnosed, not just spent — markdown reasons drafted for module 5: damaged, price match, display, expiring, goodwill — five, not thirty), password override at the two Abeokuta shops (resident supervisors), one-time codes at Lagos (the travelling approver reality, online dependency accepted and noted). Tab three: cash refund OFF at launch (store-credit-only — the conservative posture, revisited at ninety days), returns override REQUIRED with the thirty-day window, lay-by configured 15% / 3 instalments / 0-30-60 (the deposit raised from default after the MD prices the abandoned-basket risk), staff purchase enabled at the flagship only, wired to the payroll component per the Payroll track's law.

The voucher tab and the approvers (Ch. 7-8). Tab four is left DELIBERATELY conservative for module 7's launch: master switch off until the programme's accounts exist (the accountant's condition, correct), the launch design pre-agreed — Online Only, booking enforcement ON for the multi-till flagship, buy-back OFF permanently. Tab five stays empty (no integrated terminals yet — the card machine keys in manually, recorded as a decision not an omission). The approver table lands per module 1's casting: four approvers, boxes ticked per person (returns NOT bundled with discount; credit-limit override held by two only), and the go-live checklist's override rehearsal catches the module's named failure live: the second Abeokuta shop's profile required return overrides with NO approver row — the disabled-control-and-told state reproduced on the test till, the row added, the check earning its place on the permanent checklist. First sign-ins verify the landing consoles; the sidebar mirrors the constitution; and the MD's note closes the module: we argued for an afternoon about checkboxes and I realised at some point we were writing the shop's laws. Good. They were overdue.

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Common mistakes & the second law
lessons.html:
The constitution's scar tissue. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — the inherited constitution. Symptom: nobody can say which discount mode runs or why; defaults everywhere; the most permissive accident governing the margin. Disease: the profile configured by momentum, never decided (Ch. 1, 5). Fix: the walk — every consequential field converted from accident to decision, owned, recorded, and re-walked annually.

Pattern 2 — groundwork skipped. Symptom: the profile built in ten minutes and the postings unpicked for a week; the group warehouse, the wrong company, the missing tax template. Disease: the ten records assumed instead of verified (Ch. 2). Fix: the checklist in order, the sanity-check sale end to end from the back office, and the foundation priced before the furniture.

Pattern 3 — the shared template rewrite. Symptom: two counters' tax behaviour flipping mysteriously; each profile save undoing the other's. Disease: opposite tax treatments pointed at one template (Ch. 3). Fix: one template, one behaviour — each treatment its own record, and the blast radius of shared-record settings said out loud before any toggle.

Pattern 4 — the validity-window leak. Symptom: items ringing up at nil; the till flagging and the floor ignoring; margin sold at zero while everyone assumes a price. Disease: rates with lapsed windows treated as mysteries (Ch. 3). Fix: the zero-rated scan as a standing first-check, the price list's windows reviewed on selling's calendar, and the flag treated as the alarm it is.

Pattern 5 — the unguarded reverse gear. Symptom: cash refunds on from day one with no override; the drawer open in both directions; the phantom return's mechanism pre-installed. Disease: returns configured by sympathy instead of policy (Ch. 6). Fix: store-credit-first as the launch posture, cash refund as a deliberate later step with its override companion, the policy window enforced with a governed gate.

Pattern 6 — no approvers, no override. Symptom: the discount control disabled at 6 p.m. on launch day; the queue, the scene, the corridor toggle offered as first aid. Disease: override paths required but never staffed or rehearsed (Ch. 8). Fix: at least one approver per required permission, and every override path tested with a real approval on the go-live checklist before the first customer.

The second law. The counter met its system; now it has its constitution: every counter power is a profile decision with a named owner — the groundwork verified before the record exists, the tabs walked field by field, the discount mode chosen never inherited, money's reverse gear guarded, the voucher tab conservative by design, the access rows normalised and the approver table staffed and rehearsed — written where the machinery enforces it. Module 3 takes the constitution to the metal: commissioning the terminals and governing the estate.
