terminal_estate.title: POS 3 — Commissioning & the Terminal Estate
terminal_estate.desc: A terminal commissioned once and governed forever: the install and four-step wizard with the branch lock, activation and licensing by device allowance with the licence's mode precedence, the hardware layer proven with real sales, label templates and the terminal's own posture, cached cashiers with the leaver's three-record sweep and the audited manager override, and the device register with who-and-why revocation and the monthly last-seen scan.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Commissioned once, governed forever
lessons.html:
The constitution exists; now it meets the metal. This module takes a bare terminal to a counter that can take money — and then keeps taking it for years — under the module's thesis and the track's third law: a terminal is commissioned once and governed forever.

The estate frame. The reframe that organises the module: the firm's terminals are an ESTATE — a fleet of governed assets, each with an identity, a branch, a profile, a licence slot, a hardware complement, and a service history — not a pile of computers that happen to run a till. The frame imports the Sysadmin track's asset instincts wholesale: every terminal on a REGISTER (Chapter 7's device list — the platform track's access register, for machines), every change to one an EVENT (the commissioning, the repointing, the retirement — each logged with its who and why), and the estate READ on a rhythm (the last-seen scan as the fleet's dormancy check). The frame's payoff is the module's quiet promise: the manual prices the first commissioning at forty minutes and each one after at ten — and the difference is not practice alone; it is the estate discipline making every terminal the SAME governed shape, so the eleventh till is a checklist, not an adventure.

The commissioning as ceremony. The module's structure, previewed as the ceremony it is: the INSTALL and the wizard (Chapter 2 — the terminal bound to its server and LOCKED to its branch), the ACTIVATION against the licence (Chapter 3 — the terminal claiming its slot), the HARDWARE proven (Chapter 4 — the printer, drawer and display tested with real sales, not test pages), the terminal's SETTINGS and labels (Chapter 5), its PEOPLE cached (Chapter 6 — who may sign in offline, and the leaver's forget), and its REGISTER entry opened (Chapter 7 — the estate's memory). Every step produces evidence; the finished terminal has a file before it has a customer — which is this academy's oldest pattern (the ceremony whose byproduct is the documentation) at the shop floor.

The two failure modes, convicted in advance. The diseases this module prevents, named as its opening indictment: the IMPROVISED terminal (commissioned by whoever was free, named nothing, locked to the wrong branch or none, hardware half-tested — the till that works until the first return, the first offline hour, or the first dispute about which shop a sale belongs to) and the ABANDONED estate (terminals commissioned and never governed again — the retired till still holding a licence slot and a live enrolment, the lost machine nobody revoked, the device list nobody reads: the estate's version of the departed-user-with-live-access, and module 8's fraud map notes what a forgotten enrolled terminal is worth to the wrong hands). Both cured by the same two disciplines: ceremony at birth, register for life.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The install & the four-step wizard: the branch lock
lessons.html:
From installer to bound terminal — the wizard walked step by step, with the lock at its heart. The binding chapter.

The install. The pre-wizard discipline: the installer obtained and run with rights to install software — the BACKGROUND SYNC SERVICE installed alongside and set to start automatically (module 1's terminal-tied piece, born here: the service that will own the local copy and the queue exists before anyone signs in), the application launched to its unconfigured sign-in screen, and the HARDWARE connected NOW — printer, drawer, customer display plugged in and visible to the operating system BEFORE they are configured in the application (the layering discipline: the OS must see the device before the till can; Chapter 4's half of every hardware mystery is this order violated). And the manual's naming instruction, adopted as estate doctrine: name the machine at the operating-system level to match the counter — the same name the profile carries — because the device list and every support conversation for the next five years reads that name, and 'DESKTOP-7XK2P' is a filing error committed at birth.

The wizard's four steps. Server Settings from the gear icon, then: Step one — Server. The back office's full address entered WITH the protocol, then Validate & Fetch — the application contacting the server, confirming reachability, and reading back the connection details and the branch list. The failure triage taught as the manual gives it: validation fails because the address is wrong, the server is down, or the terminal has no route — check all three before continuing, in that order of likelihood. Step two — Connection. The web port, real-time path and real-time port SHOWN for confirmation — filled from the server, not editable here: if they look wrong, the SERVER is misconfigured, and the fix belongs there (the read-back design read correctly: the wizard refuses to let a terminal 'correct' the server's own facts, which is one-version law at the connection layer). Step three — Branch. The terminal's branch chosen from the fetched list and confirmed — this choice LOCKS the device to that branch — with the empty-list triage known (Reload first; a persistently empty list means the branches have no warehouse, or the address points at the wrong system), and Chapter 2 of module 2's naming discipline cashing here: branches named clearly enough that nobody picks the wrong one, because the wrong pick is discovered in postings. Step four — Updates. Automatic downloads decided (recommended ON for shops without on-site technical staff — the Sysadmin track's update-stream posture, per terminal), changeable later in settings.

The lock's governance. The design's teeth, read as the control it is: once the branch is locked, reopening server settings requires ADMINISTRATOR VERIFICATION on the terminal — deliberate, the manual says, to stop a cashier repointing a till at the wrong shop — and the academy adds the fraud-map footnote module 8 will collect: the till quietly repointed is a till whose sales land in another branch's story (the variance manufactured, the attribution scrambled), so the lock is not a convenience feature but a boundary control, its override an administrator event, logged like one. The chapter's closing line: the wizard's whole design is bind-and-verify — the terminal told once, precisely, whose it is and where it belongs — and the ten-minute commissioning the estate enjoys forever after is purchased by getting exactly that ceremony right the first time.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Activation & licensing: the slot, the lapse & the precedence
lessons.html:
The bound terminal now claims its place: activation against the branch's licence. The licensing chapter — short rules, long consequences.

Licensing by branch. The model: each BRANCH is allowed a number of devices, and every terminal records itself against that allowance the first time it signs in — the first successful sign-in REGISTERING the terminal and confirming its selling mode against the licence. The allowance's arithmetic governed like every scarce resource in this academy: the slots KNOWN (the branch's allowance and its current usage on the estate map — Chapter 7), the refusal understood (activation REFUSED when the allowance is already used, the cashier told — and the remedy being estate hygiene, not a support escalation: retire an unused terminal in the device list to free a slot, which is Chapter 7's revocation doing its daily work), and the allowance conversation held ahead of need (the new branch's terminal count is a licensing line in the opening plan, not a launch-morning discovery — the capacity-ahead-of-need instinct of the Sysadmin track's waistline, at the licence).

The lapse, handled gracefully. The design's honesty, taught because it removes a fear: if the licence lapses or cannot be validated, the terminal signs the user out GRACEFULLY — nothing is wiped and no queued sale is lost. The queue survives the lapse exactly as it survives a restart; the terminal simply stops admitting new work until the licence question resolves. The operational reading: the lapse is a commercial event with a technical symptom — the certified professional routes it to the relationship (the licence renewed, the validation restored) and reassures the counter from knowledge (the queued money is safe, the manual says so, and the professional has read the manual) rather than joining the panic.

The precedence rule. The module's most consequential single sentence, flagged in module 1 and settled here: the selling mode on the LICENCE takes precedence over the mode on the profile — a shop licensed for Standard presents the Standard console even if its profile says Pharmacy. The consequences drawn in both directions: the DESIGN direction (module 2's mode-first discipline extends upstream — the mode conversation includes the licence from the start, and the consultant proposing the two-stage counter confirms the licence carries it before the profile is built, because the profile that promises what the licence forbids delivers confusion at first sign-in), and the DIAGNOSTIC direction (the counter showing the 'wrong' consoles despite a correct profile is a licence question — the precedence rule joining the track's first-check family: profile first for missing menu items, licence next for wrong modes).

The activation ceremony. The chapter's checklist shape, closing: the slot confirmed available (or freed by revocation), the first sign-in performed by the commissioning administrator (the enrolment recorded — Chapter 7's register will carry who enrolled it and when), the mode verified as expected (the precedence rule checked live, once, at birth), and the activation noted in the terminal's estate entry. Minutes of ceremony against the alternative — the launch morning spent discovering that the allowance is full, the mode is wrong, or the enrolment belongs to nobody anyone remembers — which is the whole module's trade, made at its smallest and most frequent gate.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The hardware layer: proven with real sales
lessons.html:
The counter's physical instruments — printer, drawer, display — configured, and then PROVEN the only way that counts. The hardware chapter.

The receipt printer. The settings walked with their reasons: printing ENABLED once the printer is installed at the operating-system level (Chapter 2's layering — the OS sees it first), the MODEL family chosen (Epson or Star — the emulation families, with most thermal printers emulating Epson: the setting that decides whether the command language matches the machine), the INSTALLED printer picked from what the OS reports (Refresh after plugging in — the stale list being the commonest 'nothing prints' cause after the cable itself), the PAPER WIDTH (80mm or 58mm — wrong, and receipts wrap or clip their columns: the one-field mistake every estate makes once), COPIES (one or two — two where a signed copy is retained: an evidence policy wearing a printer setting), the PRINT FORMAT (Standard Receipt's compact thermal layout versus Invoice Style's fuller page for business customers), FONT size (paper cost against legibility on cheap thermal stock), AUTO-PRINT (off where customers usually decline — a waste policy, decided per shop), and the receipt's IDENTITY block (header name, address, footer lines, and the optional goods-return-policy text with its own switch and length cap — the counter's outward face carrying the firm's name and its return promise, owned by selling per the format-content law of the Sysadmin track).

The proving discipline. The manual's instruction elevated to doctrine: test with a REAL sale — sell a low-value item, print, then void or return it properly — because a test print does not exercise the totals, the tax lines, or the footer: the test page that looks perfect proves the cable; the real receipt proves the CONFIGURATION, and the difference is exactly the fields that matter in a dispute. The academy's addition: the proving sale is kept as the commissioning file's artifact — the first receipt stapled to the terminal's estate entry, the hardware's birth certificate.

The cash drawer. The drawer's three settings and their craft: ENABLED only where a drawer is fitted (on without one produces harmless but confusing errors — noise retired at source), the CONNECTION type read correctly (Printer for the usual arrangement — the drawer cabled to the receipt printer and opened by a pulse from it, which is why 'the drawer stopped' so often means 'check the printer cable'; Custom Command where the drawer needs its specific instruction, given as hexadecimal byte values from the drawer's own documentation; None to disable the trigger while keeping the setting), and TEST DRAWER used before going live — with the operating fact known: the drawer opens on completion of a CASH sale, which module 4's ritual relies on and module 8's fraud map watches (the drawer that opens without a sale is a read).

The pole display. The customer-facing screen's serial-line craft, taught as the diagnostic sequence it is: the PORT (Refresh to rescan after plugging in), the BAUD rate matched to the display's documentation (9600 the common default), COLUMNS and ROWS (typically twenty by two), the PROTOCOL (the command set — and the manual's precise symptom read: text appears but never CLEARS between items → choose the variant that does not send a clear command), the LINE ENDING (changed only when lines overwrite or wrap oddly), PORT LOCK (held open unless another application needs the port), and the IDLE scroll with its message (the greeting or offer between customers — the display earning its cable even when nobody is paying). The troubleshooting order adopted from the manual: garbled or overlapping text → change ONE setting at a time, starting with protocol — the one-variable discipline of every diagnostic method this academy teaches, at 9600 baud. The chapter's closing frame: the hardware layer is where the counter meets physics, and the certified professional's edge is not knowing the settings — the manual lists them — but PROVING them the real way, one variable at a time, with the evidence filed.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Labels & terminal settings: the till's own posture
lessons.html:
The remaining commissioning ground: the label templates and the terminal's System Settings — the till's own posture, distinct from the profile's policy. The settings chapter.

The five tabs. The System Settings map, oriented once: Server & App (connection status, the read-back details, the cache limit, full screen, fast checkout, updates), Printer and Display (Chapter 4's ground), Sync & Device (the cached cashiers — Chapter 6), and Labels (below) — with the constitutional distinction drawn cleanly, because it answers a standing confusion: the PROFILE holds the counter's POLICY (what may be done — module 2's constitution, central, owned by functions), while System Settings holds THIS TERMINAL'S posture (how this machine behaves — local, owned by the administrator's pen): the discount mode is a profile question; the paper width is a terminal question; and the professional who routes each to its record answers half the estate's support traffic by routing alone.

Server & App in detail. The tab's four consequential fields: the inventory cache limit (how many product rows the terminal keeps locally — raised for large catalogues where memory allows, lowered on constrained hardware, and the design consequence stated in the manual's own words and this track's standing law: anything BELOW the catalogue size means some items will not be found OFFLINE — the cache sized to the catalogue being the local-copy design's one configuration duty, and the 'item cannot be found' complaint's second check after a sync), full screen mode (title bar hidden, edge to edge — the usual choice for a dedicated till: the machine that is a till, not a computer running one), fast checkout (named here, JUDGED in module 8 — the instant-complete-and-post-in-background setting whose trade-offs belong with the queue's whole story, and the commissioning default is OFF until that judgment is made deliberately), and auto updates (the wizard's step-four decision, adjustable — the estate's update posture kept consistent across terminals, per the fleet frame).

Label templates. The shelf-edge machinery, configured on the terminal and used from the Label Printing console: a template controls the LAYOUT (name, price and barcode — or name and barcode alone), the LABEL size (width, height, and the barcode's height within it, in millimetres), the TYPE sizes (name and price point sizes), the item-code toggle, and the SHEET geometry for sheet printers (paper size, the four margins, the column and row gaps, and the column count — with zero columns meaning fit as many as the paper allows). The craft disciplines from the manual, adopted: start from a supplied PRESET and adjust (the make-vs-take instinct at the label), Save as new to keep a working template (the before-copy habit — the preset preserved, the variant named), and the proving rule in the hardware chapter's spirit: print one sheet onto plain paper and hold it against a real label sheet before committing a roll — the rehearsal that costs one page against the roll of misaligned stock every shop has thrown away once. The chapter's closing line: the terminal's own posture is small — a dozen fields and a template — but it is the layer the floor touches hourly, and the estate whose terminals share one deliberate posture (same cache logic, same update stance, same proven templates) is the estate where the eleventh till really does take ten minutes.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Cached cashiers: the terminal's people
lessons.html:
The Sync & Device tab holds the terminal's memory of its people — who may sign in when the server cannot answer. Small list, serious governance. The people chapter.

The cached list and its states. The mechanism restated from module 2's profile switch and read at the terminal: where offline login is enabled, the terminal remembers the sign-ins of cashiers who have authenticated ONLINE on that machine — and the list shows each person's state: Ready (can sign in offline right now), Re-login required (their stored credentials were REJECTED — they must sign in once while online to refresh them, and until they do their QUEUED SALES CANNOT POST: the state that links a person's credentials to the money's movement, which is why the top bar's Re-login chip is a today problem, not an admin curiosity), and Locked (more than seven days since their last successful online sign-in — offline access expired, online sign-in required). The seven-day clock's discipline, from the manual's own warning: sign in online at least WEEKLY — the cashier who only ever works through outages will eventually be locked out at the worst possible moment — and the estate's answer is a rhythm, not a memo: the weekly-online line on module 8's housekeeping calendar, owned per branch.

The leaver's forget. The lifecycle event, wired to its checklist: Forget cashier when someone leaves — the terminal no longer permits them offline — and the event read in its full shape across three records, because the leaver touches all three: the PROFILE's user row removed (module 2's table), the terminal's CACHED entry forgotten (this tab, on EVERY terminal they used — the multi-till leaver's sweep being a per-terminal walk, listed from the estate register), and the back-office ACCOUNT disabled per the Sysadmin track's lifecycle. The three-record shape is the manual's own housekeeping table given the academy's event framing: the separation checklist's counter lines, executed the same day, confirmed back to the checklist's owner — and module 8's fraud map notes the gap's worth: the departed cashier whose cached credentials survive on a back-room terminal is an offline sign-in away from an attributed-to-them queue, which is a sentence nobody wants to diagram after the fact.

The manager override sign-in. The mechanism read precisely, because its design is a control worth teaching: when an offline sign-in is refused because the terminal has no record of the cashier, a MANAGER can sign them in on the manager's own credentials — and the sales rung under the override are TAGGED FOR AUDIT, with the cashier told so at the time. The reading: the override is a continuity valve (keep a counter trading through the gap), not a routine substitute for the cashier's own sign-in — and the tag is the design keeping the valve honest: every override session is visible, countable, and attributable to the manager who opened it, so the read on module 8's page is simple (override sessions near zero, each with a story) and the drift (the branch quietly running on the manager's credentials because onboarding never cached anyone) is a silhouette, not a secret. The chapter's closing line: the cached list is the terminal's guest book — kept current by the weekly rhythm, pruned by the leaver's sweep, and never allowed to become the shared login's quiet return through the back door.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The device register: the estate's memory
lessons.html:
The module's governance layer: every commissioned terminal, on a register, for life. The estate chapter.

The register's row. What the device list holds per terminal, read as the asset record it is: the IDENTIFIER and the LABEL (the OS-level name of Chapter 2, earning its keep), the BRANCH and PROFILE it belongs to (the binding, recorded), the USER it ENROLLED as and WHEN (the activation's provenance — who commissioned this machine, on which day), and last seen (when the terminal last spoke to the back office). One row per terminal, the estate legible at a glance — the access register's sibling, for machines, and filed beside it in the site book.

Active and revoked. The lifecycle's two states and the event between them: a device is ACTIVE or REVOKED — revoked when a terminal is lost, stolen, sold or retired, with WHO revoked it and WHY recorded on the event — and a revoked device can no longer post sales. The design read for what it protects: the revocation is the estate's disable-not-delete (the history kept, the door closed), it FREES the licence slot (Chapter 3's remedy — the retirement that pays for the replacement's activation), and it is the answer to the module's opening indictment: the lost machine that was never revoked is a live enrolment in unknown hands, still able to post into the firm's story — the departed-user-with-live-access disease, in hardware, and the terminal-change line on the housekeeping calendar exists to make it structurally impossible.

Last-seen as the fleet's silhouette. The register's monitoring dividend, in the Sysadmin track's grammar: the last-seen timestamp is the quickest way to spot a terminal that has quietly stopped talking to the back office — the fleet's dormancy scan, read monthly (the manual's own housekeeping rhythm: review the device list for terminals not seen recently), with the triage taught: the stale last-seen is a closed counter (fine — noted), a dead terminal (a hardware event — the estate entry updated), or a till trading with a stopped sync service (the serious one — its queue growing unposted, its prices staling: the finding routed the day it is seen, because a till that trades without talking is accumulating exactly the backlog module 8 teaches the counter to fear). The read is two minutes against the alternative every consultant has met: the terminal discovered to have been silent for six weeks, its queue archaeology now a reconciliation project.

The estate's calendar. The module's rhythms, gathered for module 8's page: MONTHLY — the device list's last-seen review, the licence allowance's headroom glance; ON STAFF CHANGE — the leaver's three-record sweep (profile row, cached entries per terminal, account); ON TERMINAL CHANGE — the revocation with its who-and-why, the slot freed, the replacement commissioned by the ceremony; ANNUALLY — the estate walked (every row's branch, profile and label still true; the hardware complement confirmed; the commissioning files complete). The chapter's closing frame, the module's law in register form: the estate that is commissioned by ceremony and remembered by register is the estate where every terminal has a birth certificate, a current address, and — when its day comes — a death certificate with a signature: assets, governed like assets, which is all the third law asks.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: Okelewo commissions its estate
lessons.html:
Five terminals, three branches, one ceremony repeated until it is boring. Every chapter clocks in.

The first terminal: forty minutes, honestly (Ch. 2-3). The flagship's aging standalone till is replaced first. The install runs by the layering discipline (hardware connected and OS-visible before configuration; the machine named LALUBU-TILL-1 at the operating-system level — the profile's name, the estate's name, one name), and the wizard walks its four steps — with the module's promised near-miss arriving at step three: the branch list shows Okelewo Lalubu Road and the second Abeokuta shop's confusingly similar draft name, and the commissioning admin pauses exactly as trained — the branch RENAMED for clarity in the back office before the lock, not after (the wrong-pick-is-discovered-in-postings warning cashed for the price of a rename). Activation claims the flagship's first slot; the mode verifies Standard per the licence; the enrolment lands in the register with its who and when.

The licence lesson at Lagos (Ch. 3, 7). Lagos's commissioning hits the module's designed refusal: activation declined — the branch's allowance already consumed. The investigation takes one register read: an OLD trial-era terminal, dead in a storeroom for a year, still enrolled and holding the slot. The remedy is the estate discipline working as written: the corpse REVOKED (who and why recorded — 'retired hardware, storeroom, never deprovisioned'), the slot freed, the new terminal activated within the hour — and the finding generalised: the estate register's first full census runs across all three branches that week, finding one more ghost enrolment (a repaired-and-returned machine double-enrolled), the device list reconciled to physical reality before the month ends, and the monthly last-seen review added to the calendar with the ops lead's name on it.

The hardware proven the real way (Ch. 4-5). The flagship's printer configures Epson/80mm — and the proving sale catches what the test page could not: the SECOND Abeokuta shop's printer, configured by copy-paste at 80mm, is physically a 58mm machine — the real receipt's wrapped columns announcing it in one print (the one-field mistake every estate makes once, made once, on the proving sale instead of on a customer). The drawer tests fire (printer-pulse at two branches; the Lagos drawer needing its custom hex command from the documentation drawer — found, entered, tested), the pole display's garbled text yields to the one-variable sequence (protocol first — fixed on the first change), and the label template is adjusted from a preset, saved as new, and proofed on PLAIN PAPER against the label sheet — the first roll committed only after the overlay matches. Every proving artifact files into the commissioning record: five terminals, five first receipts, five birth certificates.

The people cached, the valve tested (Ch. 6). Each terminal's cached-cashier list is set deliberately at commissioning (the branch's own cashiers signed in online once, states confirmed Ready), the weekly-online rhythm lands on each branch supervisor's calendar — and the manager override is TESTED once, on purpose, at the flagship (a cashier's sign-in refused on a terminal she'd never used; the supervisor's override opens the counter; the audit tag verified visible in the back office): the continuity valve proven and its visibility demonstrated to everyone watching, which the consultant notes is the cheapest fraud-deterrence briefing the estate will ever run. The MD's commissioning-week note closes the module: the fifth terminal took eleven minutes and produced the same folder as the first. I have bought machines for nine years; this is the first time I have owned an estate.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the third law
lessons.html:
The estate layer's scar tissue. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — the improvised commissioning. Symptom: terminals named DESKTOP-7XK2P; hardware configured before the OS sees it; the branch picked from a confusing list under time pressure; no file, no first receipt. Disease: the ceremony skipped (Ch. 1-2). Fix: the commissioning checklist — OS name matching the counter, hardware layered, the wizard walked, the artifacts filed — forty minutes once, ten forever after.

Pattern 2 — the licence discovered at launch. Symptom: activation refused on opening morning; the allowance full of ghosts; the mode wrong at first sign-in. Disease: slots and precedence never in the plan (Ch. 3). Fix: the allowance and the licence's mode in the design conversation from the start, the register's ghosts revoked ahead of need, the mode verified once at birth.

Pattern 3 — the test page mistaken for proof. Symptom: the perfect test print and the wrapped real receipt; the paper width wrong across a copy-pasted estate; totals and tax lines never exercised until a customer holds them. Disease: the cable proven, the configuration assumed (Ch. 4). Fix: the real proving sale — sold, printed, properly reversed — and its receipt filed as the hardware's birth certificate.

Pattern 4 — the cache below the catalogue. Symptom: 'item cannot be found' offline; the complaint blamed on sync; the local copy silently partial. Disease: the inventory cache limit set below the catalogue size (Ch. 5). Fix: the cache sized to the catalogue per terminal's memory, and the cannot-find complaint's two-step check — sync first, cache limit second.

Pattern 5 — the stale guest book. Symptom: leavers still cached on back-room terminals; a branch quietly trading on the manager's override; cashiers locked out in the outage because nobody signed in online for a fortnight. Disease: the terminal's people ungoverned (Ch. 6). Fix: the weekly-online rhythm with an owner, the leaver's three-record sweep listed from the estate register, and the override read monthly — near zero, each with a story.

Pattern 6 — the unregistered estate. Symptom: nobody knows how many terminals exist or where; the lost machine still enrolled; the silent till discovered after six weeks with a queue full of archaeology. Disease: assets without a register (Ch. 7). Fix: the device list as the estate's memory — every terminal's row current, revocations with who-and-why, and the monthly last-seen scan that turns six silent weeks into two visible days.

The third law. The constitution met the metal, and the metal joined the books: a terminal is commissioned once and governed forever — named at birth, bound and locked by the wizard, activated against a known allowance, its hardware proven with real sales, its posture deliberate, its people cached and swept by events, and its whole life remembered on a register from enrolment to revocation. Module 4 now opens the counter's own craft: the shift and the sale — the counted float, the cart, the close.

shift_sale.title: POS 4 — The Shift & the Sale
shift_sale.desc: The cashier's module: sign-in and the top bar's grammar, the counted float and the opening's custody, the cart's craft with stack-vs-queue and the line markers, batches/serials/units with the bag-and-record discipline, the customer at the header with the credit suspend, hold-not-clear and every tender's rules, the voucher sale under the-slip-is-the-money, the lock, and the close counted, overwritten and explained — never accepted blindly.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The cashier's module: sign-in & the screen's grammar
lessons.html:
Three modules built the counter's constitution, metal and estate; this one sits in the chair. The cashier's module — the trading day from sign-in to close, under the track's fourth law: the shift is a sealed ritual — count open, count close, explain every variance. The manual's own note applies: if any part of this track is printed for the counter, it is this.

Signing in. The three doors, each with its rules: NORMAL — email and password, the till loading your profile, your catalogue and your permissions, and opening on the console you are entitled to (module 2's landing rule, felt from the chair; the forgotten password's reset link needs the terminal ONLINE); OFFLINE — where the profile enables it, sign-in against the terminal's local record: prior successful online sign-in on THIS terminal, within SEVEN days, the top bar carrying the Offline login marker, and the queued-and-post-later promise standing behind it (module 3's cached list, from the user's side — and the weekly-online habit restated as self-interest: sign in online at least weekly, or the outage locks you out at the worst moment); MANAGER OVERRIDE — the continuity valve recapped in one line: the manager's credentials open the counter, the sales are tagged for audit, and you are told so at the time — keep-trading machinery, never routine.

The top bar's grammar. The chips read as a language, because module 8 will read them as one: Online/Offline (can the terminal reach the back office), Offline login (you signed in locally — reports and lookups wait for the line), Queued (completed sales waiting to post — safe, not lost), Re-login (a cashier's stored credentials rejected — if it names you, click and refresh, or your queued sales cannot post), Conflicts (sales held back on a batch or serial no longer available — click to fix), Stock stale / Price stale (the local copies aging — click to sync now), Failed (sales the back office rejected — a supervisor's list), plus Store, Date, Time, your name and role, Duty (Active or Inactive — shown where shift management is on) with the shift button beside it, the envelope (Message Hub with its unread count), Sync (refresh now; hover shows when each copy last updated), the padlock (Chapter 7's lock), and Sign out (with confirmation). The chapter's discipline: the cashier who can READ the bar owns their terminal's state — every chip is either 'fine', 'mine to click', or 'tell the supervisor', and this module sorts them.

The console's geography. The Sales Console mapped once: products left with the search box above, the current order right; the cart HEADER carrying the customer, the item and unit counts, and — where credit checking is on — the customer's balance and limit; the FOOTER showing sales total, discount, subtotal, tax, delivery fee if enabled, and net total, with Cash and Card beneath. The sidebar lists the consoles you are entitled to (full labels wide, icon rail narrow), and beneath it the catalogue view controls: card versus LIST view (list fits far more), product images (off by default — hiding them makes the grid noticeably faster), items per row, and Recent receipts for the quick reprint. Geography learned once, then forgotten — which is the point: the certified cashier's attention belongs on the customer and the chips, not the furniture.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Opening the shift: the counted float
lessons.html:
Where shift management is enabled — and at Okelewo, per module 2, it is enabled everywhere — you must open a shift before you can sell. The module's first ritual, and the one the whole day's honesty hangs on. The opening chapter.

The mechanics. The four steps, plainly: the clock icon in the top bar opens the Open Shift window; the float is COUNTED and the opening amount entered against each payment method (cash is the one that usually matters — the others left at zero); an opening NOTE added if anything is unusual — a short float, a missing key; and Open Shift chosen, the Duty indicator turning Active. Four steps, two minutes — and the second step is the module.

Count before you open. The manual's instruction, elevated to the ritual's first commandment and taught with its full reasoning: the opening figure is what your close will be measured against — entering a round number you did not count is how variances appear from nowhere at the end of the day. The arithmetic of the sin walked once, because seeing it kills it: the drawer actually holds ₦19,400; the cashier types ₦20,000 because that is what the float 'should be'; the day trades perfectly; the close counts ₦600 short — and the evening is spent investigating a theft that never happened, or worse, NOT investigating it because 'it's always a bit off', which is the habituation that later hides the real ₦600. The counted float is custody taken properly (module 1's drawer-as-custody, in its first physical act: the signed receipt for what was actually received), and the opening note is its annotation — the short float DECLARED at open is context; discovered at close it is a dispute.

The opening's edge cases. The craft around the ritual: the float PREPARED by the ritual's logic (denominations for change-making, counted into the drawer before the door opens — the supervisor's task module 8 schedules), the handover mid-day handled as two sealed shifts (the first closed with its count, the second opened with its own — never one shift passed between hands, because a shared shift is a shared variance, and shared variances are unattributable by construction: the one-person-one-account law, at the drawer), and the shift that was never opened named for what it becomes: sales rung with no shift attach to nothing — the returns-missing-from-the-summary symptom the manual's troubleshooting table traces to exactly this, repaired after the fact only by the back-office orphaned-transactions tool (Chapter 8), which exists as a correction, not a workflow. The chapter's closing line: the open is thirty seconds of counting that buys an evening of trust — the cashier who counts before opening has pre-cleared themselves of every variance the day does not actually produce, and the supervisor who enforces the count has bought variance reports worth reading.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Building the sale: the cart's craft
lessons.html:
The trade itself: items into the cart, correctly, at speed. The craft chapter.

Adding items. The three roads: SCAN the barcode — the item added straight to the cart, and the search box does not need focus (the design fact that makes scanning uninterruptible: the cashier mid-conversation scans anyway); SEARCH by name, code or brand, then choose; TAP a tile in the grid. And the toggle module 2 configured, used from the chair: where the queue option is enabled, the switch beside the search box chooses stack mode (re-scanning the same item increases the existing line) or queue mode (each scan its own line — suiting counters where each unit needs a separate serial or batch: the electronics wall's mode, per Okelewo's own split).

Quantities and lines. The cart's grammar: each line's minus and plus buttons and the editable quantity box (type and Enter to commit, Escape to abandon — the two-key discipline that prevents the half-typed quantity from riding into payment), the bin icon removing a line — with the exceptions known and their reasons owned: bonus items, bundle components and gift voucher lines have FIXED quantities, and bundle components cannot be removed individually — remove the bundle's main line instead (the bundle price governs the parts; module 5 owns the promotion machinery, but the cart's behaviour is learned here).

Reading the line. The markers taught as the audit trail they are: Bundle on a bundle head, Rate override where the price was changed by hand (module 2's marked-for-review promise, visible), Customer discount where the customer's own recorded discount applied, and Batch assigned where batches have been picked — with the item-code toggle beside Hold showing or hiding codes per preference. The markers' discipline runs both ways: the cashier reads them to know what has happened to their own cart (the line that already carries a promotion will refuse a manual discount, and the marker says why before the refusal does), and the supervisor reads them on review (the sale whose every line says Rate override is a sale with a story — module 8's reading habit, seeded at the line).

The craft's tempo. The chapter's closing standard, because speed is part of correctness at a counter: the certified cashier's cart is built scan-first (search is the exception path), quantity-edited by keyboard (Enter committing, Escape abandoning), read by its markers before payment is touched, and never carries a line the cashier cannot explain — the ten-second review at the footer (items, counts, net total against the customer's expectation) being the cheapest dispute-prevention the counter owns: the wrong quantity caught at the cart is a keystroke; caught at payment it is a correction; caught at the door it is a return, an override, and a story.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Batches, serials & units: the tracked sale
lessons.html:
Where the goods carry identity — batches, serials, multiple units — the cart asks more of the cashier, and the asking is the control. The tracked-sale chapter.

Batch-tracked items. The flow as designed: adding a batch-tracked item, the till ASKS which batch the goods come from, showing what is available — a quantity SPLIT across batches by allocating against more than one; where AUTO-ALLOCATE is enabled (module 2's oldest-first setting), the till picks for you and only asks when it cannot cover the quantity. The mechanics' two fine points, both dispute-savers: reducing a quantity releases batch allocations in REVERSE (the last-allocated batch released first — the allocation unwound in order, not scrambled), and the Batch assigned marker on the line is clickable — review or change what was picked before payment, which is the cashier's check that the physical goods in the bag match the batches on the sale (the FEFO till that auto-picked the oldest batch while the cashier bagged from the front of the shelf is a mismatch the marker exists to catch — expiry discipline is only real when the bag and the record agree).

Serial-numbered items. The harder gate: serial-tracked items need one serial per unit — scanned into the serial window or typed — and the line will not proceed to payment until every unit has a serial. The gate read as the control it is: the serial binds THIS physical unit to THIS sale (the warranty claim, the return, the recall all resolve to it — the Inventory track's identity law at the counter), so the gate that feels like friction at 6 p.m. is the record that settles the dispute in March — and the certified cashier scans serials from the UNITS IN THE BAG, never from a convenient box on the shelf, because a serial record that does not match the goods handed over is worse than none: it is confident fiction.

Units of measure. The multi-unit ask: where an item sells in more than one unit — each, pack, carton — the till asks WHICH unit applies, and the price follows the unit chosen. The craft point: the unit ask is a pricing event (the carton price against twelve singles is a margin design someone made in module 2's groundwork), and the mis-picked unit is the counter's quietest large error — the carton sold at the single's price is an eleven-twelfths discount nobody approved, invisible until the margin report, which is why the footer's ten-second review from Chapter 3 explicitly includes units on multi-unit lines.

When the pick is refused. The concurrency truth, taught calmly: a batch or serial can be REFUSED — another till may have sold it in the meantime — and the answer is simply to pick a different one. If the sale has already completed and been held back, it appears under the Conflicts marker in the top bar: module 8's territory, previewed in one sentence — the conflict is the local-copy design being honest about a race it lost, the fix is a re-pick, and the discipline is that conflicts are cleared before the shift closes, because a conflicted sale is money that has not reached the ledger. The chapter's closing line: the tracked sale is the counter carrying the warehouse's laws at retail speed — the ask is the control, the marker is the check, and the bag and the record leaving together, agreeing, is the whole point.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The customer at the header: attach, loyalty & credit
lessons.html:
A sale with no named customer books to the walk-in customer — correct for most of the queue. This chapter is the rest: the named customer, attached properly, with everything that follows. The customer chapter.

Attaching. The mechanics: the person icon above the grid, or the customer chip on the cart header; SEARCH by name, phone or email and select — with the offline behaviour known (the search runs against locally CACHED customers when the line is down: the local-copy design covering the customer file); CREATE where new — name, and mobile and email if held (module 2's duplicate-name refusal and the mobile-match auto-merge standing behind the create, keeping eleven cashiers from minting eleven spellings of one woman); and the LOYALTY road — tick Issue loyalty card and scan or type the number at create, or, for an existing member, scan their loyalty card from the scan button above the grid: the customer loads automatically and their points appear on the header. The attach's effects, immediate and automatic: any discount recorded on the customer's record APPLIES (the Customer discount marker from Chapter 3 — recorded policy, not counter generosity), and where credit checking is on, the balance and limit appear on the header.

The credit suspend. Module 2's fence, met from the chair: a customer over their limit shows Sales suspended due to customer outstanding — and payment is blocked until an approver releases it. The cashier's script taught, because the moment is social before it is technical: the suspend is read to the customer as the system's fact, not the cashier's judgment ('the account needs a supervisor before I can add to it' — the fence taking the blame, which is what fences are for), the release is the Power Approver's credit-limit permission doing its work (an authorised event, logged), and the cashier never routes around it — the full-cash alternative is offered where the customer prefers it (a paid sale needs no credit release), but the part-paid workaround, the split-across-two-tickets improvisation, is module 8's fraud map wearing a helpful face.

Loyalty's counter half. The points machinery from the cashier's side: earning happens by attach (the member not attached earns nothing — the attach habit IS the programme), redemption happens at payment (Chapter 6 — online only, because the balance lives on the server), and the returns interaction is previewed for module 5: where an original sale earned points that were since SPENT, the return computes what must be recovered and shows it before completion — the cashier explains it from the screen, never estimates it. And the header's last discipline, closing the chapter: the customer attached is attached for the WHOLE sale — the mid-sale attach applies the customer's discount to what is already in the cart correctly, but the attach forgotten until after payment is a loyalty dispute and a reprint request rolled into one, so the certified habit is attach-first for any customer who mentions membership, before the first scan.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Hold, clear & payment: money's minute
lessons.html:
The basket parked or discarded, and then the money itself — every tender, in one chapter. The payment chapter.

Hold, do not clear. The pair distinguished by what survives: Hold parks the basket and empties the cart for the next customer — held baskets KEEP their customer, discounts and batch allocations, resumed from the box icon above the grid (which shows the count), aged out automatically where module 2's housekeeping is on. Clear DISCARDS the basket — and where the cashier is not permitted to clear but an approver holds the permission, the button still appears and asks for approval (the authorised-discard design, per the constitution). The manual's rule is the chapter's title and the counter's habit: the customer who walks off to fetch their wallet gets a HOLD — clearing throws away the batch and serial work already done, and, per module 8's map, the clear that follows a cash-in-hand moment is a pattern the supervisor reads, so the honest counter simply never builds the habit.

Cash and card. The two buttons beneath the totals: CASH — the tendered amount entered (or a quick-amount button), change calculated and displayed, completion opening the drawer and printing per configuration; CARD — without the integrated terminal, the amount simply RECORDED (the card machine worked as usual, then confirmed); with integration, the amount PUSHED to the terminal and the till waiting for the result (module 2's gateway, live).

Split payment. One bill across several methods: Split payment on, a method chosen and its portion entered, Add another method per further portion, the REMAINING balance watched as it falls — with the over-tender rule known precisely: if CASH is among the methods, over-tendering shows change due; WITHOUT cash, the total may not exceed the amount owed. Complete when the remaining balance reaches zero. The craft note: split is the counter's honest answer to real wallets (some cash, some transfer) — and every portion lands on its own payment method for the close's per-method count, which is why the cashier who records a transfer as 'cash to balance faster' has just manufactured two variances from one sale.

The server-side tenders. The three that need the line, each with its reason: Loyalty redemption — Redeem Loyalty Points, the programme picked, the points entered, their cash value deducted (the balance lives on the server; offline it cannot be trusted, so it cannot be spent); Gift vouchers — added from the payment window's voucher section, scanned or typed, each reducing the amount due, MORE than one applicable, full coverage asking no further tender, surplus handled by the profile's change policy (module 7 owns the programme; the tender behaviour is learned here); Store credit — chosen as a split method, the available credit shown, an amount above it refused. And the offline capability recap, in one breath because module 8 owns the full table: cash, manually keyed card and transfer work offline; integrated card, store credit, loyalty redemption, anything voucher, and any credit or part-paid sale do not — offline, you collect the full amount, because a balance that reads nil cannot be checked.

Back-dating. Where module 2 permitted it: a transaction date field at the top of the payment window, today or earlier only — used for the genuinely late-rung sale, marked by its nature (revenue moved between reporting days), and rare by policy. The chapter closes at the footer: payment is the sale's seal — every tender on its own method, every server-side tender honest about the line, and the remaining balance at zero the only way out.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Receipts, the voucher sale & the lock
lessons.html:
The sale's paper, the counter's one bearer-instrument moment, and the padlock. The evidence chapter.

Receipts and reprints. The paper's rules: auto-print printing on completion where configured (one or two copies), otherwise printed from the confirmation; the RECENT RECEIPTS panel (from the catalogue controls) for the quick reprint of the last few sales; Sales History (module 6) for anything older. And the offline reference law, restated from module 1 because the chair is where it matters: a sale completed offline prints with a LOCAL reference — once posted, the back-office reference takes over — both refer to the same sale, and a return can be found by either: the customer's offline receipt is not a second-class document, and the cashier says so with confidence when asked.

Selling a gift voucher. The counter's most careful sale, walked step by step: the gift voucher TILE on the grid; a face value from the denomination buttons or another amount typed; the quantity set; for PRE-PRINTED stock, each physical card SCANNED so the code binds to the value — for system-issued vouchers, codes left blank and generated on completion; added to the sale (same-value vouchers grouping onto one line — the fixed-quantity line from Chapter 3); payment taken with the tender rule absolute: vouchers are bought with cash-equivalent tenders only — never with another voucher, store credit, or loyalty points (stored value does not mint stored value — the closed loop that prevents value appearing from nowhere, and module 7 will give the rule its accounting spine). A NAMED customer is required (the voucher may need emailing or reprinting later); no email on file prompts for one, skippable — in which case the printed slip is the only copy. And the manual's warning, this chapter's engraving: the slip is the money — the full code appears on the printed slip exactly once, a reprint requires authorisation, and an unissued slip is treated like cash, because to its bearer it is.

Locking the till. The padlock's contract: lock IMMEDIATELY on stepping away — the shift stays open, the basket stays as it is, synchronisation continues — unlocked with username and password. The habit argued once, then assumed: the lock is faster than signing out and back in, it protects the open basket (the batch and serial work, the attached customer), and it protects the CASHIER — the unattended, unlocked till trading under your name is your variance, your overrides, your story, whoever's fingers made it; the lock is the one-person-one-account law defended sixty times a day, in one keystroke. The chapter's closing frame: this is the module's evidence layer — the receipt that survives offline, the slip that is money, the lock that keeps your name yours — and none of it costs ten seconds.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The close & Okelewo's first trading month
lessons.html:
The ritual's second seal, and the case study's first month at the new counters. The closing chapter.

Closing the shift. The steps, with the module's second commandment inside them: the clock icon opens the Close Shift window — total sales, returns and transaction count for the shift, plus lay-by bookings, payments and refunds where there were any; the counted amounts arrive PRE-FILLED with what the system expects for each payment method — and the manual's emphasis is the academy's: do not accept them blindly. The drawer and each method are COUNTED, each figure OVERWRITTEN with what was actually counted; the per-method VARIANCE shows beside each — green over, red short — with a total at the foot; variances EXPLAINED in the closing notes; Close Shift chosen, Duty turning Inactive. The commandment's reasoning, taught plainly: the pre-filled figure accepted untouched is not a count — it is the system agreeing with itself, a reconciliation with one side, worth nothing on the evening the drawer is actually short; the counted close is the custody handed back with a signature, and the variance EXPLAINED at close ('₦200 over — suspected change error on a busy split sale, noted at 4pm') is context that costs a sentence, where the same variance unexplained is Monday's investigation.

The unclosed shift. The failure mode and its repair: an unclosed shift leaves the sales unattributed and forces a supervisor to reconcile after the fact; a missed shift is REPORTED — the back-office tool attributes orphaned transactions to the shift they belong to (the manual's own correction path, and the troubleshooting table's answer to returns-missing-from-summaries) — a correction, never a workflow, and module 8's calendar makes the pattern visible if it tries to become one.

Okelewo's first month (every chapter clocks in). The counters trade governed for the first time, and the month produces exactly the module's lessons: the COUNTED FLOAT catches its first prize in week two — the flagship's Tuesday drawer opens ₦1,500 light against the prepared float, declared in the opening note, and the discrepancy resolves to the weekend's change-making raid on the float box (a process fix: the float sealed after preparation), where the old counter would have discovered it at close and argued about it for an hour; the HOLD habit saves a serial sale in week three (a customer fetches a wallet; the held basket resumes with three scanned serials intact — the old counter would have rebuilt it or, worse, guessed); the pre-filled-close commandment survives its first temptation (a rushing Saturday cashier accepts the pre-fill once — the supervisor's review catches the untouched figures the same evening by their perfect roundness, and the re-count, done together, teaches the lesson better than the memo would have: ₦350 over, real, unexplained because uncounted); the month's variance report reads as designed — small, explained, attributable per cashier per shift — and one cashier's consistent small SHORTS on split-payment days trace not to theft but to Chapter 6's exact sin, transfers rung as cash 'to balance faster', corrected by a five-minute retrain; and the first VOUCHER sale drills the slip-is-money rule before December's programme (a pre-printed card scanned, bound, sold to a named customer with an email — the slip handed over with the sentence the consultant scripted: 'keep this like cash; the code is on it once'). The MD's month-end note: for nine years the drawers were 'about right'. This month I know, per shift, per person, per method — and the arguments have simply stopped. The counting turned out to be the cheap part.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the fourth law
lessons.html:
The ritual's scar tissue. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — the round-number float. Symptom: variances from nowhere; the ₦600 investigation of a theft that never happened; 'it's always a bit off' as culture. Disease: the opening figure typed, not counted (Ch. 2). Fix: count before you open — the float prepared and sealed, the opening note declaring anything unusual, the custody taken with a real signature.

Pattern 2 — the shared shift. Symptom: one shift passed between hands; variances nobody can own; the handover mid-basket becoming handover mid-drawer. Disease: two custodies under one seal (Ch. 2). Fix: two sealed shifts — the first closed with its count, the second opened with its own — one person, one account, one drawer, one variance.

Pattern 3 — the fiction serial. Symptom: serials scanned from the shelf box, not the bag; warranty claims that resolve to units the customer never held; the record confident and wrong. Disease: the gate satisfied instead of used (Ch. 4). Fix: serials from the units in the bag, the batch marker reviewed against what was actually bagged, the bag and the record leaving together in agreement.

Pattern 4 — the cleared basket. Symptom: batch and serial work thrown away for a wallet trip; the clear that follows cash-in-hand moments; rebuilt carts and guessed allocations. Disease: clear where hold belongs (Ch. 6). Fix: hold, do not clear — the parked basket keeping its customer, discounts and allocations; the clear an authorised, watched event.

Pattern 5 — the tender shortcut. Symptom: transfers rung as cash 'to balance faster'; two variances from one sale; per-method counts that fight the drawer. Disease: the tender's truth traded for speed (Ch. 6). Fix: every portion on its own method — the split machinery used as built, because the close counts per method and the shortcut manufactures the very variance it was dodging.

Pattern 6 — the blind close. Symptom: pre-filled figures accepted untouched; perfect-looking closes with nothing behind them; the real short discovered weeks later, unattributable. Disease: the system agreeing with itself and calling it a count (Ch. 8). Fix: do not accept them blindly — count, overwrite, explain; the variance with a sentence at close instead of an investigation on Monday.

The fourth law. The counter's day, sealed at both ends: the shift is a sealed ritual — the float counted before the door, the cart built by craft and read by its markers, the tracked sale's bag and record agreeing, every tender on its own method, the slip treated as the money it is, the till locked whenever the chair empties, and the close counted, overwritten and explained — never accepted blindly. Module 5 opens the counter's pressure valve: concessions, returns and overrides — everything that takes money off or gives money back.
